ice.c: ICE: In TheFVorkj of the Learned for Ju ’ y,. there is an Abridgment of a French Book, called Nouvelle Conjecture four expiquer la Nature de la Place; in which the Nameless Author modestly proposes the following Conjectures about Freezing and lee. Water Freezes only because its Parts lose their Natural Motion, and cleave close to one another; but we must observe, . That the Water, whilst it Freezes, seems to dilate it self, and that it becomes more light; whereas it should seem that it ought to become more weighty. . That Frozen Water is not quite so transp - rent, and that the Bodies transpire not so freely through it as formerly; tho ’ one would think the contrary should happen, if it be true, that the Wa - ter dilates it self as it Freezes. These are the seeming Contrarieties which are found in the Ef - sects and Properties of Ice, that make the Nature of it obscure and difficult to be explained. Tis the common Opinion of Philosophers, That tee is made by certain Spirits of Nitre, which in the Winter mix with the parts of the Water, and being of themselves improper for Motion, because of their Figure and Inflexibility, enfeeble and de - stroy gradually that of the parts to which they are joined. This Opinion is supported by fqjne Experiments, which prove, at least, that on certain Occasions the Spirits of Salt and Nitre contribute to form the Ice. ' ' Our Author has no Design to controvert those Experiments: He says only, That ’ tis not certain thar the Spirits of Nitre do always enter into the Composition of Ice; And that though they enter ’ d the fame constantly, that alone would not be fuffi - cent to explain all the Effect. Forlnftance; We cannot conceive how the Spi - rits of Nitre, which enter the Pores of the Water, and fix the parts of it, can oblige the Water to di - late it self, and make it more light; whereas Natu - rally they ought to augment the Weight of it, This Difficulty, and some others that might be inlisted upon, shew theNeceffity of anew System to ex - plain the Nature of Ice: Therefore our Author gives this that follows, which he conceives explains all things with more ease, and in a more simple man - ner, than the ordinary System. He alledges. That Water Freezes in the Winter, because its parts being more closely joined together, they mutually embarrass one another, and lose all the Motion they had; and he supposes the Air to be the some, or at least the principal Cause, why the parts of the Water join so closely together. He ex - plains it thus: There is an infinite Number of small parts of gross Air mixt among the parts of the Water, as every Man may plainly perceive; for if we put in - to a Pneumatick Machine an open. Vessel full of Water, in that fame proportion as you pump the Air out of the Machine, you will see the Water bubble up, and fend forth a great Quantity of gross Air. These ICE Those parts of gross Air being dispersed among those of the Water, they have each of them the Vertue of a Spring; which is now so well proved in Natural Philosophy, that no Man will call it in question. If then it can be ( hewed. That the small Springs of gross Air, mixed with the Water, have moire Force in the Winter, and that then they unbend themselves a little - y it would easily be conceive ’ d, that on one Side those Springs unbending themselves in that manner, and on the other the external Air continuing to prels the Surface of the Water, the parts of the Water ( hut up betwixt those small Springs which repulse them on all Sides, mud needs be locked up one against another, ice their Moi - fture, and form a hard Body that is to fay, Ice. All the Difficulty lies in this, How to know whether in reality the Springs of the Air, which are dispersed in the Water, unbend a little in the Winter, which his. easy to prove they do. The gross Air, which we cannot perceive in the Water whilst it is liquid, is easily seen when ’ tis Frozen We fee then very often a great quantity of Bubbles of Air very sensibly and when they are too small to be observed every one apart, we may fee them confusedly and in gross; for frozen Water is always a little whiter than ’ twas before and they that have studied any thing of the Nature of Colours, know that this Whitenels proceeds on - ly from the small Bubbles of Air mix ’ d with the Ice. This is the Reason that all Scums are whitish, and that the Bubbles of Air mixed with Glass or Chry - stal, appear whiter than the reft. Add to this, That the little Bubbles of gross Air, which are absolutely insensible in the Water, so long as ’ tis liquid, cannot become sensible in Frozen Wa - ter, but because each of them becomes grosser than they were: And they cannot become grosser, but for one of these Reasons Either because the Wa - ter, when it Freezes, hath attracted new Air or because the Air already dispersed in the Water, takes up a greater Space, and that its Springs are a little more unbended. We cannot conceive how the Water, as it Freezes, could attradfc new Air, since the Pores of the Ice are certainly less than those of the Water, thro ’ which the gross Air cannot pass but with Difficulty. It mull be then, that the Air al - ready dispersed among the Parts of the Water is di - lated, and that the Springs are a little unbended. But why, when ’ tis Cold, have the Springs of the Air more strength to unbend themselves, than at a - nother Season ? It is answered in the First place, That to establish this System here laid down, it is enough to prove that the thing happens. really so, without any necks - licy. pf explaining the Cause of it. Secondly, That this Cause is not very difficult to be found, Every one knows that Bodies with Springs have so much more Force as they are more stiff; and that they are so much the more stiff, as their Pores are less; but it ’ s the Property of Cold to reftridf the Pores: And during the Heat the Pores are more open, because the subtil Matter which pas - fes always through them, being then in a more vio - lent Motion, hath the more Force to extend them and keep them open; whereas in the Winter, their Motion being much ( lackened, all the Bodies ( hut themselves up, and their Pores are strained. Hence itxomes, that in the Winter the Bodies of Animals transpire much less than in another Season., Since then the Cold locks up the lead Parts of the gross Air, and makes them less pliable and more stiff, be - cause it straitens the Pores we must fay also, that I CE it augments the Force of their Springs, the Springs becoming more violent, according as the Body be - comes more stiff, Thus, during the Winter, the Springs of Air which are dispersed in the Water, having confide - rably more Force, they must unbend themselves a little, and as they unbend, they press against one another the small Parts of Water which they hold ( hut up. This being supposed there ’ s nothing in Ice but what may be explained Naturally enough. . That Water, as it Freezes, ought to make a hard Body, because then its Parts being pressed one against another, they embarrass one another mutu - ally, aud so lose all the Motion they had. . That Water, as it Freezes, ought to become more light; for tho ’ its Parts be more press ’ d than they were before, yet the Mafe being composed of the Parts of the Water thus press ’ d, and of Air di - lated, ought to be more large, and by consequence more light, than it was when the Water was liquid. . Frozen Water takes up a greater Space than when ’ tis liquid, because the Springs of Air difp'er - fed in the Water, by unbending themselves, do oblige the Water to rife in the Vessel which con - tain ’ d it. It is true, that the external Air presses also the Surface of the Water, and makes an Ef - fort to repel it; but this external Air being freer, and its little Springs less bended, because they un - bended themselves according as the Cold lock ’ d up the neighbouring Bodies, it hath less Force than that which is ( hut up in the Water, whole Springs cannot unbend, but by making the Bulk of the Wa - ter larger. . If you ( hut up a Vessel full of Water in the Pneumatick Machine, the Air dispersed in the Wa - ter dilates it self in an extraordinary manner when they pump the Air of the Machine - let the Water Freezes not, because the external Surface of the Water being no more press ’ d, the Air which it con - tains may, by unbending it self, escape freely, as in reality it does. . Frozen Water must always be left tranlpa - rent than the fame Water when it is liquid, because the Bubbles of Air which are insensible in the Wa - ter, by reason of their Smallness, being more sensible and large in the Ice, must also make it appear to be more white, and by consequence left transparent. . The Bodies must much left transpire through the Ice than through the Water, because the Parts of the Frozen Water, are, in Effect, more press ’ d than they were before, and so leave a left free Passage to foreign Bodies. . The Water, from which there ’ s abundance of Air drawn by means of the Pneumatick Engine, must also Freeze with less Difficulty - of which an able Man told our Author he had made the Experiment. . The Spirit of Wine, Brandy, and other Li - quors of the lame fort, cannot Freeze at all, or at least rarely j for their Parts being in a great Moti - on, as appears by the Evaporation made of them, it follows, thatthe Air dispersed into the Parts of thole Liquors, is much more subtil, and by consequence hath less of a Spring, than that which is dispersed; in the Parts of common Water, since the Spring of the Air is principally in its gross Parts. . Oil, Fat, and other vilcous Liquors, must: congeal more easily than Water Freezes, because their Parts being improper for Motion, do Ipeedily embarrass one another; but thole Liquors, when they congeal, cannot become so hard as Ice, nor di - N late themselves in the fame manner - for though they, contain contain among their Parts a greater Quantity of Air than Water does, yet that Air is more subtil, hath Ie ! s Spring, and easily makes its way through the Pores of those Liquors. . Quicksilver cannot Freeze, because it does not contain a great enough Quantity of groIsAir; its Parts also are much polish ’ d, and they can easily Hide one against another, without embarraffmg or j flopping one another. . According as the Cold grows more sharp, I the Springs of the Air dispersed in the Ice, ought to have more Force to repel the Parts of the Frozen Water j and the Bulk composed of the Air and Frozen Water must needs grow larger and larger. This hath been prov ’ d in the following manner: They fill ’ d with Water an hollow Iron - Bullet, which had a Hole of three or four Lines Diameter; the Water being Frozen in that Bullet, and not be - ing strong enough to break it, the Ice issued at the Hole, and form ’ d a fort of Stalk or Ice - fickle, which lengthened according as the Cold increased, and grew to the Length of a Finger; this Stalk be - ing broke, and the Bullet exposed to the Air during a very Cold Night, it made a new Stalk, but not so long as the former, the Ice's pining it self, if we maybe allowed so to speak, as it paded through the Hole of the Bullet; as Gold and other Minerals do, by passing through the Wire - drawer ’ s Instru - ments;,... iz. In the Hypothesis here laid down, the Spi - rits of Nitre may also contribute to form the Ice, in as much as by joining themselves to the final ! Parts of the Air dispersed in the Water, they contribute towards rendring them more stiff and inflexible, and to augment the Force of its Springs. idea.c: IDEA, is whatsoever the Mind perceives in it self, or stands there for the immediate Objecft of any Phantasm, Notion, Species, Thought or Un - derftanding.

IDEA ’ S. Our Observation employ ’ d, either about External Ob j efts, or about the Internal Q - operation of our Minds, perceived and reflected only by our selves; is that which supplies our Under - standing ( faith Mr. Loci with all the Materials of Thinking. These Two are the Great Sun - tains of Knowledge from whence all the Idea ’ s, Notions, Phantafms, Species, &c. which we have, or can naturally have, do spring and arise. . Our Senses, being conversant about parti - cular Sensible Objects, do convey into the Mind several diftindf Perceptions of things: And this way we gain the Idea ’ s of Tellow, White, Heat, Cold, Soft, Hard, Bitter, Sweet, and all those which we properly call Sensible Qualities, and this Great Source of molt of the Idea's we have, de - pending wholly on our Senses, and derived by them to theUnderftanding, is called Sensation. . The other Fountain from which Experience furnishes the Understanding with Idea ’ s, is the Perception of the Operation of our own Minds with - in us, as it is employed about the Idea's it hath before gotten by Sensation: Which Operations, when we come to EefleB and Confider on, our Un - derftanding thereby becomes furnish ’ d with ano - ther Set of Ideas, which could not be had from things without; and such is Perception, " Thinking, Doubting, Believing, Beafoning, Knowing, Wit - ling, &c. and all the different Actions of our Minds; which we being conscious of, and ob - serving in our selves, do from these receive into our Underftandings, as diftinB Idea ’ s, as we do from Bodies affeding our Senses. This is a kind of Internal Sensation; is called very properly, by Mr. Loci, fieflettion: And these two, Sensation and Befleftion, he takes to be the only Originals from whence all our Idea's take their Beginnings. And so far the Mind or Understanding is meer - ly passive; and cannot choose whether it will have these Beginnings or Materials of Knowledge or not. he Objects of Sense will obtrude their I - dea's upon our Minds; and the Operations of our Minds will not let us be withoutfome ( atleaft ob - feure ) Notions of them. No one can be wholly ignorant of what he doth when he Thinks: And as the Mind is forced to receive Imprefiionsfrom without, so it cannot avoid the Perception of those Ideas that are annex ’ d to them ? Vol. II. I D E Of Idea's, some ( as we should carefully ob serve ) are Simple, and others Complex. All those Idea's that come into our Minds by Sensation, are of the former kind: And tho the Qualities in Bo - dies that affedour Senses are in the Things them - selves, so united and blended, that there is no Se - pacation nor Distance between them; yet the I - dea's they produce in the Mind enter by the Senses simple and unfix ’ d. Some Idea's come into our Minds only by one Sence, which is peculiarly a - adapted to receive them: As the Idea's of all Co - lours are received only by the Eye; z Sounds and Tones by the Ear, &c. Heat, Cold, and Solidity, by the Touch. Other Idea ’ s we gain by more than one Sence; as of Space, Extension, Figure, Be ft, and Motion For these make forcible Impreffions both on the Eyes and Touch. There are other Simple Idea's which convey themselves into the Mind by all the ways of Sen - fation and ftefleBion; as Pleasure, Pain, Power, Existence, Unity, and Succeftion; and these are all, or, at least, the most considerable of those Simple Idea's which the Mind hath; and out of which is made all its other Knowledge. To underhand the Nature of these Simple I - den's the better, and to discourse of them intelli - gibly, it will be convenient to distinguish them as they are Idea's or Perceptions in our Minds, and as they are Modifications in the Bodies that cause such Perceptions in us; that so w e may not thinly ( as perhaps is usually done ) that they are exactly, the Images t and ftefemblances of something inhe - rent in the Subject: For most of those of Sense - tion are in the Mind no more the Likeness offome - thing existing without us, than the Names that hand for them, are the Likeness of otto Idea's. But here the Qualities in Bodies, which produce these Idea's in our Minds, must be distinguished into Primary and Secondary. Primary Qualities are such as are utterly in separable from the Body, in what State soever it be; such as the Sence constantly finds in every Particle of Matter; which are So - lidity, Extension; Figure, Motion, test, and Num - ber. Secondary Qualities are such as are in reality Nothing in the Gbje & s themselves, but only Powers to produce various Senfations in us by. their Primary Qualities; i. e. by thzBulk., Figure, Texture, and Motion of their Insensible Parts; as Colours, Sounds, Tasts,, &c. Now the Idea's of ' Primary Qualities are, in feme fence, Iffemb lances of them, and their Patterns do really exist in the Bodies themselves; but the Tfej ’ j produced in us by these Secondary Qu alities have no ftefemblance of them at all. There is nothing like our Idea ’ s existing in the Bodies themselves: They are in the Bodies, we denominate from them, only a Power to produce those Senfations in us: And what is Sweet, Blue, ox Warm in Idea, is but the cer - tain Bulk, Figure, and Motion of the insensible Parts in the Bodies themselves, which we call so. here are several Faculties which the Mind hath of managing these Simple Idea's, which are very well worth our Observation; as that of Differ - ning duly, and rightly Distinguishing one from ! another: In this consists the Accuracy of Judge - H h h ment. D E merit, and the avoiding all Confufions and Mi - stakes. a. That of Comparing them one with another, in respect of Extent, Degree, lime, Place, or any other Circumstances of Relation or Dependance one on another. . The Faculty of Compounding or putting to - gether the Simple Ideas receive ’ d by Sensation or RefleBion, in order to make Complex ones. . " When Children, by repeated Senfations, have got ( omeldea's fix ’ d in their Memories, they, by degrees, begin to learn the Use of Signs and when they can Ipeak articulately, they make use of Words to signifie their Ideas to others: And the Use of Words being to stand as outward Marks of our Internal Idea's and thole Idea's being ta - ken from particular things, if every particular Idea that we take in should have a particular Name. Names must grow endless. To prevent this, the Mind, by, . Another Faculty, can make the Particular Idea's received from such Objects, to become General: Which is done by conlldering them as they are in the Mind such Appearances, separate from all other Exiftences, and the Circumstances of real Existence such as Time, Place, or any o - ther concomitant Idea's and this is called Ab - JlraBion whereby Idea's taken from particular things, become general Reprefentatives of all of that kind j and their Names, General Names ap - pliable to what ever exist conformable to such AbfiraB Idea's. Thus the fame Colour being ob - serve ’ d to Day in Chalk or Snow, which the Mind Yesterday received from Milk, or CeruJJe it con - friars that Appearance alone makes it a Repre - fentadve of all of that kind and having given it the name of fVhitenefs, it by that found signifies the fame Quality wheresoever to be met with or imagined. And thus ZJniverfals, whether Idea ’ s or Terms, are made. From the Power which the Mind hath of com - binding thus, comparing, and separating or abjlra - ing its Simple Idea's, which come into it by Sen - fat ion and Reflection, all Complex Idea s are form d and, as before in the Perception of Idea's, the Un - derstanding was paflivc, so here tis above; ever - ting the Power it hath in the several Ads and Fa - culties above - mention ’ d, in order to frame Com - pounded Ideas. All Complex Ideas, tho ’ their Number be infi - nite, and Variety endless may be, as it seems, all reduce ’ d to these three Heads, vi. Modes, Sub - stances and Relations. Modes are such Complex Idea's, which how e - ver compounded, are not supposed to exist by themselves, but are considered as Dependencies on, or AffeBions of Substances: Such are the Idea's signified by the words Triangle, Gratitude, Mur - ther, ( c. and these Modes, as Mr. Lock calls them, are of two forts. . Such as are only Variations, or different Combinations, of the fame Simple Idea, without the Mixture of any other as a Doyen, a Score, &c. and these may be called Simple Modes. I D E z. There are others compounded of Simple I ", dea ’ s of several kinds put together to make one Complex one as Beauty, Theft, ( c. Substances have their Idea's such Combinations of Simple Idea ’ s, as are taken to represent distend particular things fubfifting by themselves; in which thefuppofed, or confuled Idea ofSubftance such as it is, is always the First and Chief. Relations, are a fort of Complex Idea's ’ arising from the Confidcmtion ind. Coziip & rtion of one J - dea with another. Of these, some depend only on the Equality orExcefs of the fame Simple Idea in leveral Subjects and these Mr. Lock thinks may be called Proportional Relations such as equal, more, bigger, ftweeter, ( c. Another Oc - casion of comparing things together, is the Cir - cumftances of their Origin or Beginning - and this being not afterwards to be altered, make the Relations depending thereon as lasting as the Subjeds to which they belong: These are Natu - ral Relations, such as Father, Brother, Vncle, Cou - fins, ( c. There are also Relations by Institution, as Prince and People, General and Army, ( c. Mo - ral Relations, are the Conformity or Disagree - ment of Men ’ s free Adions to Laws and Rules, whether Divine or Human. It may be considered also further about our T - dea s, that some are clear and diftinB; others obscure and confused. Our Simple Ide is are clear when they continue such as the Objects rere - sent them to us, when our Organs of Sensation are in a good Tone and Order when our Me - monies retain them, and can produce and present them to the Mind when ever it hath occasion to confider them p And if along with this the Mind fees that these Simple Idea ’ s are severally different one from another, and each single one from all the reft. then they are distend also as well as clear: And the contrary to this will occasion Obfcurity and Confufton.

identitatenominis.c: IDENTITATE NOMINIS, is a Writ that lies for him, who upon a Capias or Exigent, is taken and committed to Prison for another Man of the Name,

ideota.c: IDEOTA inquirenda vel examinanda, is a Writ to the Escheator or Sheriff of any County, where the King hath Notice that there is an Ideot, Natu - rally Born, so weak of Understanding, that he cannot govern or manage his Inheritance, to call before him the Party suspected of the Ideocy, and examine him; and also by the Oath of Twelve Men, to enquire whether he be sufficiently Witted to dispose of his own Lands with Discretion, or not, and to certify accordingly into the Chancery: For the King hath the Protection of his Subjects, and by his Prerogative, the Government of their Lands and Substance, that are Naturally Defective in their own Discretion.

ides.c: IDES of a Month, among the Romans, were the Day after the Nones were out They commonly fell our on the th of every Month, except in March, May, July, and OBober ( which they called the Full Months, as all the others were called Hol - low ) for then they were on the th, because in those. Months the Nones were on the th. The E - etymology of the Word is variously given, and to be seen in most Dictionaries: See Danets Greeks and Roman Antiquities.

idiocrasy.c: IDIOCRASY, the proper Disposition or Tem - perament of a Thing or Body.

idiopathy.c: IDIOPATHY, is a primary Disease, which new - ther depends on, nor proceeds from any other.

idiosyncrasy.c: IDIOSYNCRASY, is a Temperament peculiar to any particular Animal Body; whereby it hath, either in Sicknels or in Health, a peculiar Aversion against, or Inclination for some particular things; or on which some things will have no such, or a more than usual Operation, than they will have on other Bodies.

jeerorjeer.c: JEER, or Jeer - Rope, is a Piece of a Hawser fa - ttened to the Main - yard and Fore - yard ( in great Ships only close to the Ties then ’ tis reeved thro ” a Block, which is seized close to the Top, and so comes down again, and is reeved through another Block at the Bottom of the Mast close by the Deck; there are usually two of these, one on each Side the Ties. Its Ule is to help hoyse up the Yard, but more especially to succour the Ties, and to keep the Yard from falling, if they should break.

jejunumintestinum.c: JEJUNUM Intestinum, is the Second of the small Guts, so called, because it is most times found empty: ’ Tis in Length about eight Foot in Men; it begins on the Right Side under the Colony where the Duodenum ends, and fills a good Part of she Umbilical Region, especially on the Left Side I L E I M B tis continued, to the Ileum, but is easily known from it by its Emptiness, by the great Number of its Veins and Arteries, which make it look a little Red - dilh, and'aifo because the Wrinkles in its Coats are more in number, and nearer to one another, than those in the Ileum, and the Coats themselves are much thicker.

jeofailincommonlaw.c: JEOFAIL, in Common Law, signifies an Over - fight in pleading, touching which you have a Sta - tute, AT... whereby it is ena & ed, That if the Jury have once past upon the Issue, tho ’ after - ward there be found a Jeofail in the Pleading, yet Judgment shall likewise be given, according to the VerdiCl of the Jury.

jessant.c: JESSANT, when in a Coat of Arms a Lion or other Bead: is born over some Ordinary, as over a Chief, a Bend, a Sense, &c. that Lion or Beast is blazoned JeJfant or Jacent, i. e. lying over all.

jet.c: JET D ’ EAU, is the French Word for a Pipe of a Fountain which calls up the Water any, consider - ble Height into the Air. Mr. Mariotte, in his Treatise du Mouvement des Faux, &c. faith. That a Jet d ’ Eau will never rife so high as its Reservatory, but always falls short of it by a Space, which is in a subduplicate Ratio of that Height and this he proves by several Experiments. He faith also, That if a greater branches out in many smaller ones, distributed to different Jets, the Square of the Diameter of the Main Pipe must be proportioned to the Sum of ail the Expences of its Branches; and particularly faith, That if the Re - fervatory be a Foot high, and the Adjutage half an Inch in Diameter, the Pipe ought to be Inches in Diameter. ignoramusinlaw.c: IGNORAMUS, in Law, is a Word ufedby the Grand Inquest, impannelled in the Inquisition of Causes Criminal and Publick, and written upon the Bill when they dislike their Evidence, as des - active or too weak to make good the Presentment: TheEfteClof which Word so written is, That all farther Enquiry upon that Party, for that Fault, is thereby stopped, and he delivered without further Answer.

ile.c: ILE, is the Cavity from the Thorax to the Bones of the Thighs: Pliny observes. That all the Inte - ftines in all Animals, except a Man and a Sheep, are called He. Blanchard.

ileum.c: ILEUM, is the Third of the Small Guts, so cal - led zero rr Hhci d. r, a Circumvolvendo, because of its many Turnings, &c. It begins where the Je - junum ends, and ends it self at the Gut called Cae - cum, at the beginning of the Colon: It is about Hands Breadth in Length: There can be no such thing as willing of the Guts, but sometimes the Coats being doubled inward, the upper part of an Intestine links ar falls with the lower, which makes the IliackcPaJJion, or Volvulus. The Ileum oft falls down into the Scrotum, and then the Rupture is cal - led Inteftinalis. The Passage of the Ileum is a little narrower then that of the Jejunum f and its Coats are somewhat thinner.

impetigocelsi.c: IMPETIGO CELSI, the fame with Lepra Gr.. torum, Celfus makes four lorts of it: The molt harmless, says he, is that which is like a Scab, for it is red and hard, exulcerated and gnawed: But it differs from it, in that it is more exulcerated, and is accompanied with speckled Pimples: And there ieem to be in it certain Bub - bles, from which after a certain time there fall, as it were little Scales, and it returns more certainly. Another fort is worse, almost like a fort of Mea - zles, or - hot Pimples in the Skin,, but more rugged, and redder, and of different Figures: In this Di - temper little Scales too, fall from the Surface of the Skin, and it is called Rubrica. The third fort is yet worse; for it is thicker and harder and wells more, and is cleft on the top of the Skin, and gnaws more violently: It is Scaly too, but black, and spreads broad and flow: It is called Nigra. The fourth fort is altogether incurable, of a dis - ferent Colour from the Red; for it is something white, and like a fresh Scar, and has pale Scales; some whitish, some like the little Pulse called Lin - tel, which being taken away, sometimes the Blood follows: Otherwise the Humour that flows from it is white, the Skin hard and cleft, and spreads farther. All these forts arise especially in the Feet and Hands, and infest the Nails likewise. Impetigo some reckon the fame with Lichen. Blanchard.

INCLINATION of a Plane, in Dialling, is the ' Arch of a Verticie Circle, perpendicular to both she Plane and the Horizon,, and intercepted between ihem. To find the Inclination of a Plane. Take a Quadrant, and apply its Side to the Side f a Square, and apply the other side of your Square to your Plane if the Plummet fall parallel to the Side of the Square, then the lower Side of the Square stands level; by which draw an Horizontal Line, whereon ered a Perpendicular, and apply your Square to that Perpendicular, and if the Plum - met falls parallel to the Side of the Square, then that is also a level Line, and your Plane stands Horizontally: If the Plummet falls not parallel to the Side of the Square, then turn your Square until it does, and draw an Horizontal Line, on which ered a Perpendicular, to which apply your Square, and observe what Angle your Plummet makes on the Quadrant, with the Side of the Square that is, the Angle of the Inclination of the Plane

individuum.c: INDIVIDUUM; in Logicl is that which figni fies but one only thing: Of which they make a fourfold Division. . Individuum Determinatum, is when the Thing is n am d or determined as Alexander, the River Nile, or Mount Athos. This also is called Signatum. . Individuum Demonfirativum, is when some Demonstrative Pronoun is uled in the Expression as this Man, that Woman. . Individuum ex Hy pot heft, or by Suppolltion when an Universal Name or Term is restrained by the Suppolition to a particular Thing; as when we lay, the Son of such an one, and it be known that he had but one Son.

indivisiblesingeometry.c: INDIVISIBLES, in Geometry, are filch Ele - ments or Principles as any Body or Figure may ul - timately be resolved into. And thele Elements, or Indivisibles, are in each peculiar Figure supposed to be infinitely small. With regard to which Notion, a Line may be said to consist of Points; a Surface of Parallel - Lines, and a Solid of Parallel and Similar Surfaces: And then, because each of these Elements is supposed In - divisible, if in any Figure, a Line be drawn thro the Elements perpendicularly, the Number of Points in that Line, will be the fame as the Number of the Elements. Whence we may fee, that a Parallelogram, Prism, or Cylinder, is resolvable into Elements, or Indivi - fibres, all equal to each other, parallel, and like to the Base. A Triangle into Lines parallel to the Base, but decreasing in Arithmetical proportion, and so are the Circles which constitute the Parabolicl - Co - void, and those which constitute the Plane of a Cir - cle, or the Surface of an Iloceles Cone. A Cylinder may be resolved into Cylindrical Curve Surfaces, having all the fame height, and continually decreasing inwards, as the Circles of the Base do, on which they insist. This Method of Indivisibles, is only the Ancient Method of Exhauflions a little disguised and contra - cted: It was fitft introduced by Cavallerius in his Geometria Indivifibilium, Anno Dorn.. purfu - ed after. by Torricellius in his Works, Printed. and again by QavaUerm himself in another Trea - dle, published. And is now allowed to be of excellent Use in the fliortening of Mathematical De - monftrations: Of which take the following Instance in that Famous Proposition of Archimedes, That, A Sphere is two thirds of a Cylinder eircum ' ascribing ite For suppose ( as in the Figure ) a Cylinder, He - mifphere, and an Inverted Cone, to have the fame Base and Altitude, and to be cut by Infinite Plane ? all parallel to the Base, of which d g is one: ’ Tis plain, the Square of dh will every where be equal to the Square of IQ C ( the Radius of the Sphere ) the Square h c eh Square; and consequently, since Circles are to one another, as the Squares of the I N D Radii, all the Circles of the Hemisphere will be equal to all thole of the Cylinder, deducing thence Ik i / " / s all those of the Cone: Wherefore the Cylinder, de - ducking the Cone, is equal to the Hemisphere; but tis known, the Cone is one third of the Cylin - der, and consequently the Sphere must be two thirds of it.. E. D.

induction.c: INDUCTION, is commonly taken. for the gi - ving polfeftion to an Incumbent of his Church, by leading him into it, and delivering him the Keys, by the Commissary or Bishop ’ s Deputy, and by his ringing one of the Bells.

INDUCTION. When a Clerk is Instituted into a Benefice, he is to exhibit his Mandate from the Bishop to the Arch - Deacon, or other Person to whom it is directed; and hath a Right thereby to be Induced into his Living; and if he be refused Induction, he hath a Remedy both in the Ecclesiastical Court, and also an Action of the Case in the Common Law, against the Arch - Deacon. If the InduBor, or Person to be Indu - cted, be kept out of the Church or Houfeby Lay - Men, the Writ de vi Laid lies for the Clerk; which is direCted out of the Chancery to the She - riff of the County, to remove the Force, &c. If another Clergyman, presented by the fame Patron, keep Possession, a So iation is grantable out of the Spiritual Court; whereby theTythes, ( c. shall be sequestered till the Right be determined. The Arch - Deacon rarely InduCts a Clerk by hinafelfin Person, but Flues out a Warrant to all Clerks and Letter ’ d Persons within the Arch - Dea - cowry, imbowering any of them to do it in his stead. The usual Form and Manner of Induction is, for the InduBor to take the Clerk by the Hand, and then to lay it on the Key of the Church, which must be then in the Door, and to fay. By Vertue of tins Instrument, which is the Arch - Dea - cons Warrant, I InduB you into the Real, ABual, and Corporal Pojfejfton of the Rectory or Vicarage of A. with all its Fruits, Profits, Members, and Ap - purtenances: This done, he opens the Door, and puts the Clerk in Possession of the Church, and shut - s the Door upon him; who after he hath tolled a Bell ( if there be any ) comes our, and defires xht InduBor to endorse a Certificate of his InduBion on the Arch - Dcacon ’ s Warrant, and mat all present will signifie it under their Hands. If the Church Key cannot be had, ’ cis fuffident that the Clerk lay hold of the Ring of the Door, and within the time limited read the Common - Prayer and Thirty Nine Articles in the Church - Porch. If there be no Church he may lay his Hand on the Wall or Fence of the Church - Yard, &c. there being no necessity of Niceness as to the Form of InduBion; only that he must have Wit - less that he was truly possess ’ d of it. Within two Months after this the Clerk must read the Thir - ty Nine Articles, and all the Service of the Day both at Morning and Evening Prayers; and de - clare his Assent and Consent; and he must then also read the Bi ( hop ’ s English Certificate, in which is the Declaration of his Conformity; and of all this he must have two or three good Witnesses; Vol. II. I N F who must Sign that they heard him do it, and be ready to attest it viva voce, if required: And within three Months after InduBion he must take also the Abjuration Oath, at the Quarter - Seffipns, or in some one of the Courts in W'eftminfter.

inequalityofnaturaldays.c: INEQUALITY of Natural Days. Tho the Sun is supposed Vulgarly to measure ourTime e - qually, yet he is very far from doing so: And as tis impossible for a good Clock, or Movement, to keep time with the Sun; so one that is truly such, will measure Time much more truly, and go exa & er than any Sun - Dial. The usual Reason, and one good one it is, of the inequality of Natural Days, you have under the Word Equation of Time: But the Truth is, there is also another; and that is, That the Motion of the Earth it self round its Axis, is not exactly Equable or Regular, but is sometime swifter, and some times flower... t.,

infernal.c: INFERNAL - STONE, or Perpetual Cauftick., is a Chymical Operation, whereby Silver is rendred Caufticiby the Salts of Spirit of Nitre. Tis thus made: Dissolve in a Viol any Quantity of Silver in thrice its Weight of Spirit of Nitre; and then in a Sand - heat evaporate f - of the Moisture: The Remainder put into a good large German Crucible, which place over a gentle Fire; let the Matter alone, and hea - ving till at last it finks quietly to the Bottom: Then increasing the Fire a little, ’ twill turn into an Oil j If I N D and as soon as you perceive it to be so; it must ini - j mediately be poured into an Iron - Mold, purposely I made sot it, that is a little ois and greas ’ d, where it will presently coagulate and harden. After ' tis taken out, it must be kept in a Viol well stopt; ' tis a great Cauftick, and will last for ever, if it be kept from the Air. Some make them of Copper, but those are not so good as these.

infinite.c: INFINITE, is that which has no Bounds; Terms, nor Limits.

infinitequantity.c: INFINITE QUANTITY, Of the several Species of Infinite Quantity, and of the Proportions they bear one to the other, the Learned Mathematician Capt. Halley, in Philofoph. Tranfadbions, N. X, gives the following Account. That all Magnitudes infinitely great, or such as exceed any assignable Quantity, are equal among themselves, though it be vulgarly received for a Maxim, is not yet lo common as it is erroneous and the Reason of the Mistake seems to be. That the Mind of Man coming to contemplate the Ex - tenfions of what exceeds the Bounds of its Capaci - ty, and of which the very Idea does include a Ne - gation of Limits; it comes to pals, that weacqui - sce generally, and it suffices to fay, such a Quan - tity is Infinite. But if we come more nearly to examine this No - tion, we shall find, that there are really besides In - finite Length, and. Infinite Area, no less than three several forts of Infinite Solidity: All of which are Quantitates sui generis, having no more Relation or Proportion the one to the other, than a Line to a Plane or a Plane to a Solid, or a Finite to an In - finite; but that among themselves each of these Species of Infinites, are in given Proportions, is that which is to be made plain. But first. Infinite Length, or a Line infinitely long, is to be considered, either as beginning a Point, and so infinitely extended one way, or else both ways from the fame Point; in which case the one which is a beginning Infinity, is the one half of the whole, which is the Sum of the beginning and cea - sing Infinity, or of Infinity a parte ante, and a parte post, which is analogous to Eternity in time or dura - tion, in which there is always as much to follow as is past from any Point or Moment of Time: Nor doth the Addition or Subducftion of finite Length or Space of Time alter the case, either in Infinity orE - eternity, since both the one and the other cannot be any part of the whole As to Infinite Surface Or Area, any Right Line in - finitely extended both ways on an infinite Plane does divide that infinite Plane into equal parts, th J one to the right, and the other to the left of the said Line: But if from any Point in such a Plane two Right Lines be infinitely extended, so as to make an Angle, the infinite Area, intercepted between those infinite Right Lines: is to the whole infinite Plane:: as the Arch of a Circle, on the point of Con - course of those Lines as a Centre, intercepted be - tween the said Lines: is to the Circumference of the Circle; of as the Degrees of the Angle, to the a Degrees of the Circle. For Example. Two Right Lines meeting at a Right Angle, da include, on an infinite Plane, a quarter part of the whole infinite Area of such a Plane. Btit. TZCfi ) I N F But if so be two parallel infinite Lines be. suppo - fed drawn on such an infinite Plane, the Area in - tercepted between them will be likewise infinite; but at the Tame time will be infinitely less than that Space which is intercepted between two infinite Lines that are inclined, tho with never so small an Angle; for that in the one case, the given finite Di - stance of the Parallel Lines, diminishes the Infinity in one Degree of Dimension; whereas in a Sebtor, there is Infinity in both Dimensions; and conse - quently the Quantities are the one infinitely greater than the other, and there is no proportion between them. Froth the fame Consideration arise the three fe - veral Species of infinite Space or Solidity, as has been said; for a Parallelopipid or a Cylinder infi - nicely long, is greater than any Finite Magnitude how great soever; and all such Solids supposed to be formed on given Bases, are as those Bases, in proportion to one another: But of these three Di - mentions are wanting, as in the Space intercepted between two parallel Planes infinitely extended, and at a finite Distance; or with infinite Length and Breadth with a finite thickness; all such Solids hall be as the given finite Distances one to another; but these Quantities, tho ’ infinitely greater than the other, are yet infinitely less than any of those wherein all the three Dimensions are infinite. Such are the Spaces intercepted between two inclined Planes in finitely extended; the Space intercepted by the Sur - face of a Cone, or the Side of a Pyramid likewise infinitely continued, &c. of all which, notwithftand - ing the proportions one to another, and to the vast Abyss of infinite Space, ( wherein is the Locus of all things that are or can be; or to the Solid of infinite Length, Breadth and Thickness taken all manner of ways ) are easily assignable. For the Space between two Planes: is to the whole:: as the Angle ol those Planes: to the Degrees of the Circle. As for Cones and the Pyramids, they are as the Spherical Surface intercepted by them, is to the Surface of the Sphere; and therefore Cones are as the Versed Sines of half their Angles to the Diame - ter of the Circle. These three forts of Infinite Quan - tity, are analagous to a Line, Surface, and Solid, and after the fame manner cannot be compared, or have no proportion the one to the other. Besides these, there are also several other Species of Infinite Quantity, arising from the Contemplation of Curves, and their Asymptotes, which he leaves to the Speculation of the Learned Mathematicians.

infinitive.c: INFINITIVE - MOOD, in Grammar, is when a Verb is used so as to determine neither any parti - cular Person, or Number. INFLAMMATION: See Phlegmone.

inflation.c: INFLATION, is the Diftentation of a part from Flatulent Matter.

inflection.c: INFLECTION ( in Opticks ) is a Multiplicate Refraction of the Rays of Light, caused by the one - qual Density of any Medium, whereby the Motion or Progress of the Ray is hindred from going on in a Right Line, and is InfleCted or DefleCted by a Curve, faith the ingenious Dr. Hoof, who first took notice of this property in his Micography, p.. And this he faith, differs both from Reflection and RefraCtion, which are both made at the Superficies of the Body, but this in the middle of it within. Sir If. Newton, as you will find under the Word Light, discovered also by plain Experiment this Inflection of the Rays of Light; and Mr. De la Hire, faith he found, That the Beams of the Stars being observed in a deep Valley, to pals near the I N F Brow of an Hill, are always more refraCted than if there were no such Hill, or the Observations were ' made on the Top thereof as if the Rays of Light were bent down into a Curve, by palling near the Surface of the Mountain. See Vol..

influences.c: INFLUENCES of the Planets, or HeaVenly Bo - dies, are such Physical Powers or Forces, as they are supposed to have on Sublunary Things.. Mr. Boyle is inclined to believe ( tho ’ he had no Opinion of Judicial Astrology in other, refpears ) that the Planets may have Tome Physical Influence or - operation on Bodies belonging to our Globe, from thele Considerations.. That it cannot be denied, - that; all the Affe & i - ons and Dispositions of Moisture, Hear, Cold, Drought, the Course of all Winds, Showers, Thun - der, &c, and whatever else helps to produce the great and universal Esse & s of Rarefaction and Con - sensation in our Atmosphere, do in a great Measure, if not entirely, depend on the Motion, Position, Si - tuition, and Afpedts of the Superior Celestial Bodies or Planets. That every Planet hath its own proper Light distinct from every other, which Light not being a bare Quality, but designed for a further use than meer Illumination, must be accompanied with some peculiar Tincture, Virtue, or Power.. z. That this Light of each particular Celestial Body, not being at all Refracted in theEtherial Spa - ces, it is transmitted thro ’, descends entirely and uncharged into our Atmosphere. . That whatever is received into our Atmo - sphere, is also received by the Thin and Subtile Air, which is contiguous to the Atmosphere; which cannot but be capable of being moved, stirred, al - tered, and influenced by these differently disposed Lights which penetrate each part of it. . And since the Thin and Subtile Air is capable of being thus affected, moved and altered by these Planetary Virtues, it must needs variously impress, . move;. - agitate and infect the Spirits or Subtiler parts of all Bodies within its reach; and; confequendy must have a coofiderafctle influence upon: the Bo - dies wherein such Spirits reside, and whom they actuate.. - This is also farther confirmed,, as true in Fact, by those sudden strokes of Cramps Convulsions, Elites, Colds, Pestilential Invafions, which do not only often, as it were in an instant, seize oh pur Bodies, but which do alio continue for a long time, c c. IN FORMA PAUPERIS, in Law, is when any Man that hath a just Cause of Suit, either in the Chancery, or any other of the Courts of Common Law, Will courie eitfPer before the Lord Keeper, iVIafter bf the Rolls,. either of the Chief Jiiftices, or Chief Baron, and make Oath that he is not worth five Pounds, his Debts paid, either of the said Judges will in his own proper Court, admit him to sue in forma Pauperis, and he shall have Council, Clerk or Attorney assigned to do his Business, without paying any Fees.

informatusnonsum.c: INFORMATUS NON SUM, or rather non sum Informatus, in Law, is a formal Answer made of Course by an Attorney; that is, commanded by the Court to fay what he thinketh good in defence of his Client; who being not instructed to fay any thing material, says. He is not informed, by which he is deemed to leave his Client undefended, and so Judgment passeth for the Adverle Party.

informedstars.c: INFORMED STARS, are luch of the Fixed - Stars, as are not Call: into, or ranged under any Form. See Spof des.

infusion.c: INFUSION, is an Extraction of the Vertue of Medicines with a convenient Liquor, which if it be Purgative, it is usually taken at one Dose; and to this the Name properly agrees.

ingredients.c: INGREDIENTS, are the several Parts or Sim - ples that go to the making of any Compound Me - divine; and in general it signifies the Constituent Parts or Principles of a mixt Body.

ingressinastronomy.c: INGRESS, in Astronomy, signifies the Sun ’ s en thing the first Scruple of one of the four Cardinal Signs, especially Aries.

ingressu.c: INGRESSU, is a Writ of Entry, whereby a Man leeketh Entry into Lands and Tenements: It lies in many Cafes, and hath many several Forms; See Entry. This Writ is also called in particular, Pracipe aud reddat, because those be formal Words in Writs of Entry. The Writs, as they lie down in divers Cafes, are these, fet down in the Old Nat. Brev.

INGRESSU ad communem Legem, is a Writ which lieth where a Tenant for Term of Life, or of another Life, Tenant by Courtesie, or Tenant in Dower, maketh a Feoffment in Fee, and dieth r. He in Reversion shall have the aforesaid Writ a - gainst whomsoever that is in the Land after such Feoffment made. I & GRESSU'ad ' a Writ Which Heth where the Lands ' or Ten'efiiehtaf are Lee to I N O I N J to a Man for Term of Years, and the Tenant hold - eth oyer his Term.
INGRESSU causa Matrimony prcelocuti: See Causa Matrimonii pralocuti.
INGRESSU cut ante divortium See Cut ante di - ver tium.....

INGRESSU dum non suit compos mentis, is a Writ which lies when a Man felleth Land or Tene - nant, being out of his Wits,
INGRESSU in casu consimili: See Casu confi -
INGRESSU in casu prove / o: See Casu proviso.

ingressujuper.c: INGRESSU Juper dijfeifna in fe quibusfvs, a Writ which lies where a Min is disseised, and dieth, for his Heir against the Dilfeilor..

ingros.c: INGROS S AT OR magni Rotuli: See Cleric of the Engrosser, in Common Law, is one that buys Corn growing, or dead Victuals, to fell again. Also a Clerk that writes Records or Instruments Of Law in Skins of Parchment.

ingrossing.c: INGROSSING of a Fine, is making the Index - tures by the Chirographer, and the Delivery of them to the Party unto whom the Cognizance is made.

inguen.c: INGUEN, is that place from the Bending of the Thigh to the Secret Parts. ‘ INHARMONIC AL Relation, a Term in Musick: Sec Relation Inharmonical. INHERIT AN CE, is a Perpetuity in Lands or Tenements to a Man and his Heirs: For Littleton, lib. i. cap. i. says, This Word Inheritance is not on - ly understood where a Man hath Inheritance of Lands and Tenements by Descent of Heritage, but also every Fee - simple or Fee - tail that a Man hath by his Purchase, may be said by Inheritance, for that his Heirs may inherit after him.

inhibition.c: INHIBITION, is a Writ to inhibit or forbid a Judge from further proceeding in the Cause depend - ding before him: See F. N. B. Sol. - where Pro - hibition and Inhibition are put together. But Inhi - sition is most commonly a Writ issuing out of a high - er Court - Christian to a lower and inferior; and Prohibition out of the King ’ s Court to a Court - Chri - sivan, or to an inferior Temporal Court.

injection.c: INJECTION, is the casting ( by a Syringe, & c. ) feme liquid Medicine into Wounds or Cavities of the Body, or of the Vessels; Clyfters are hence by some called Injections. Several Experiments have been made about

injectionofliquors.c: INJECTION of Liquors into the Veins of Ani - mals, from whence probably some good Hints may be taken; I shall therefore mention some of them. Sir Fraxafiati, Professor of Anatomy at Isa in Italy, injeded a little Aqua Fortis diluted into the Crural and Jugular Vein of a Dog, and he died presently; and had ( on opening him, ) all his Blood found fixed, except about the Guts: Some of th great Vessels were burst. Some Spirit of Vitriol being injected into the Veins of another Dog, he died not so soon, but fetched his Breath thick and difficultly; and foamed like an Epileptick; but dying at last, he opened him, and found his Blood fix ’ d in the Veins Grumous and like Soot. Oil ' of Tartar invested, did not kill the Dog, tho tried upon him several times; but he grew more eager for Meat than before, and getting some Bones he gnawed them most greedily. Oil of Sulphur injeCted, swelled the Dog and oil - led him; his Blood was found not coagulated, but more thin and florid than ordinary: Which Confti - tuition, perhaps, may be as fatal in the Blood, as its being curdled and fixed.

injunction.c: INJUNCTION, is a Writ grounded upon an Interloquotory Order in Chancery; sometimes to give Possession to the Plaintiff, for want of the De - fendant ’ s Appearance,; sometimes to the King s Or - finary Court, and sometimes to the Court - Chri - ftian, to stay Proceedings in a Cause upon Sugge - stion made. That the Rigour of the Law, if it take place, is against Equity and Confidence in that Case.

inium.c: INIUM, is the Beginning of the oblongated Marrow, which is the common Sensory, because the Species which are received from the external Organs are conveyed thither by the Nerves. Blan - chard.

inlagaryaterminlaw.c: INLAGARY, a Term in Law, signifying a Re - ftiturion of one Outlaw ’ d to the King s Protedion and to the Benefit or Estate of a Subject

innateprinciples.c: INNATE Principles, according to feme Philofe - phers, are primary Notions or Charaders which they will have to be stamp ’ d upon the Mind of Man when it first receives its Being, and which it brings into the World with it.

innominata.c: INNOMINATA tunica oculi, the Tunick of the Eye that wants a Name, is a certain fubtleEx - panfion of the Tendons, from the Muscles which move the Eye to the Circumference of the Iris or Horney Membrane.

INNOMINATA OJfa, are two large Bones ft. mated on the Sides of the Os Sacrum, and in a Fee - tus may each be separated into three Bones, Ilium Os Pubis, and Ischium, joined by Cartilages and appear distend by three Lines till seven Years ’ old but grow all into one Bone at riper Years; they are by feme called Cuneiformia.

innominatushumor.c: INNOMINATUS Humor, or Injit us, is a Se condary Humour, as the Ancients call ir, wherewith they thought the Body was nouriffied: For those Nutritious Humours they talked of are four, Into - - minatus, Ros, Gluten, Cambium. Blanchard INNOTESCIMUS, fin Law ) are Letters Pa - tents which are always of a Charter of Feoffment or feme other Instrument not of Record and so fti led in the Words of the Conclusion, Innotefcimus per presented.

inns.c: INNS - OF - COURT, are lo called, because the Students there Study the Laws, to enable them to praise in the Courts of Wefiminfter, or elsewhere, These are the Middle and Inner - Temple, Lincolns - Inn and Grays - Inn. There. are also two Serjeants Inns, and eight Inns of Chancery.

innuendo.c: INNUENDO, is a Word frequently used in Writs, Declarations, and Pleadings; and its Use is only to declare and afeerrain the Person or Thine which was named or left doubtful before.

inoculation.c: INOCULATION, is a kind of Grafting by the Insertion of the Bud of one kind of Fruit - Tree “ into I N S into the Bark of another, so as to make different Kinds of Fruit grow on the fame Tree, and the fame common Sap supply them all.

inquirendo.c: INQUIRENDO, is an Authority given to aPer - fon orPerfons, to enquire into something for the King ’ s Advantage.

inquisitioninlaw.c: INQUISITION, in Law, is a manner of pro - ceeding in Matter Criminal, by the Office of the Judge, or by the great Inquest before Justices in Eyre.

inquisitors.c: INQUISITORS, are Sheriffs, Coroners, super visum corf oris, or the like, who have Power to en - quire into certain Cafes.

inrolmentinlaw.c: INROLMENT, in Law, is the Regiftring, Re - j cording, or Entnng of any Lawful AdHnthe Rolls i of the Chancery, as a Recognisance acknowledged, j or a Statute, or a Fine levied j or in the Rolls of j the Exchequer, King ’ s - Bench, or Common Pleas; or in the Hustings of London, or by the Clerk of the j Peace in any County.

insaniaoramentia.c: INSANIA, or Amentia, Madness, is an Aboliti - on or Depravation of Imagination and Judgment.

insconsedaterm.c: INSCONSED, a Term in the Art Military, im - plying that a Part of an Army hath fortified them - selves with a Sconce or small Fort, in order to de - fend some Pass, &c. See Sconces.

inscribedingeometry.c: INSCRIBED, in Geometry, a Figure is said to be inscribed in another, when all the Angles of the Figure inscribed touch either the Angles, Sides, or j ! Planes of the other Figure.

Oj T, which signifie the Dodecahedron, Sphere, Icofiihedron, Cube, Octahedron, and Tetrahedron.. The Vfies of these Lines may be these. I. The Radius of, a Sphere being given, to find the Sides of the Five Regular Bodies infcrilfid in it, , The Side cf any of the Five Regular Bodies given, to find the Radius of the Circum - / bribing Sphere, If the Sphere be first given, apply its Radius over in the Points S, Si on each Leg of the Senior, If any of the other Bodies be first given, apply its Side over between its proper Letters; so the Parallel taken between the Points of the other Bodies, stall be the Sides of those Bodies, and may be inscribed in the Sphere, whose Radius is the Distance between S and S.

insessus.c: INSESSUS, is a Bath for the Belly, proper for the lower Parts, wherein the Patient fits down to the Navel. They are for several Uses, as for easing of Pain, foftning of Parts, dispelling of Flatulent Matter, and frequently for exciting the Courses. Blanchard.

insimultenuit.c: INSIMUL Tenuit, is one of the Species of the Writ called Formedon; which lee.

insistingtheangles.c: INSISTING, the Angles in any Segment, In Geometry, are laid to be inffiing upon the Arch of the other Segment below.

insitionthebotanickwordforgrafting.h: INSITION the Botanick Word for Grafting
insitionthebotanickwordforgrafting.c: INSITION, the Botanick Word for Grafting it signifies in general, the insertion and uniting of any I Cyon, Bud, &c. into the Substance of the Stock, ! and is of divers Kinds.

insolation.c: INSOLATION, is exposing of any Body to be warmed or heated by the Beams of the Sun.

inspeximus.c: INSPEXIMUS, are Letters Patent, so called because they begin, after the King ’ s Title, with this Word Infteximus; and is the fame with Exemplifi - cation. '

inspiration.c: INSPIRATION, is an alternate Dilatation of the Chest, whereby the Nitrous Air is communicated to the Blood, to accend it by the Wind - pipe and its Vesicular Parts. The Cause of Inftiration doth notfeem to consist only in ’ the Dilatation of the Thorax, as is common - ly thought, but also in the Contraction of the Tu - mick, which covers the upper part of the Oesophagus, and the inst close Receffes of the After a Arteria. Blanchard.

instant.c: INSTANT, is such a part of Duration wherein we perceive no Succession; oris that which takes up the Time of only one Idea in our Minds, without the Succession of another, wherein we perceive no Succeffionat all.

institutionsorinfiitutes.c: INSTITUTIONS, or Infiitutes, Part of the First of the Four Tomes or Volumes of the Civil Law; and is a Compendium of the Digest drawn into Four Books, composed on purpose by the Em - peror for the Use of young Students; that so having I N T the first Elements of the whole Profeffton in this lit - tle Treatile, they might the sooner gain a compel tent Knowledge of it, without being discouraged by the Largeness of the former Books. INTACTiE, are Right Lines, to which Curves do continually approach, and yet can never meet with them: These are usually called Asymptotes which fee,

integers.c: INTEGERS, from the Latin Integrum, signifies in Arithmetick whole Numbers, in Contradi & ion to Fractions.

intension.c: INTENSION, is a Writ that lies against him that enters after the Death of Tenant in Dower, or other Tenant for Life, and holds him out in the Reversion or Remainder: And every Entry upon the Possession of the King, is called an Intension; as where the Heir of the King ’ s Tenant enter af - ter Office, and before Livery; this is called an In - tension upon the King.

intensioninnaturalphilosophy.c: INTENSION, in Natural Philosophy, signifies the increase of the Power or Energy of any Qua - lity, such as Heat, Cold, &c. for of all Qualities, they fay, they are Intended and Remitted; that is, capable of Increase and Dimuninon. Under the Word Quality you will find it demonstrated, That the Intension of all Qualities increases reciprocally, as the Squares of the Distances from the Center of the Radiating Quality decreases.

intentionorstudy.c: INTENTION, or Study, is when the Mind with great Earnestness, and choice, fixes its View on any Idea, considers it on all Sides, and will not be called off by the ordinary Solicitation of other Ideas.

intercalary.c: INTERCALARY - DAY, is the odd Day put in or inserted in the Leap - Tear..

intercepted.c: INTERCEPTED - AXE, a Term in Conick Se - ctions, signifying the fame with Abscissa which fee.

intercolumniation.c: INTERCOLUMNIATION, is the Space or Distance between the Pillars of any Building.

intlrcolumnsor.c: INTLRCOLUMNS, or Inter calumniation, In Architecture, are the Spaces between Column and Column in any Portico or great Piazza, I c.

intercostal.c: INTERCOSTAL - ARTERIES, are Arteries, ac - cording to some, so called, because they go to the Regions about the Ribs: The upper bestows it self among the Muscles that are between the four highest Ribs; and the under one goes to every Muscle that is between the reft of the Ribs.
INTERCOSTAL - VESSELS, are the Veins and Arteries that run along the Intervals or Spaces of the lower and upper Ribs; on which Account they are distinguished into Superior and Inferior.

intercostales.c: INTERCOSTALES extern & intern, are Mu scales placed in the Intervals of the Ribs, as their Names declare. Their Number on each Side is twice eleven, equal to the Interfaces in which they are lodged. Their Originations are different - ly assigned by Anatomists; but ’ tis most probable that they do arise from the lower Edge of each fu - period Rib, and are inserted to the upper Edge of each inferior one. These are thin and fleshy; the Fibres of the External pass from above obliquely downwards to the Fore - part, or OJfa Pubis: Thole of the Internal descend in like manner obliquely towards the Back - parr, or Os So - um, their Fibres decussating each other like the Letter X.

interjectioningrammar.c: INTERJECTION, in Grammar, is an indecli - table Word used in a Sentence, to declare the Af - sections or Passions of the Mind, and to compleat the Sense of it.

interlocutoryorder.c: INTERLOCUTORY Order, is that which de - cides not the Cause, but only fettles some intervene - ing Matter relating to the Cause; as where an Or - der is made by Motion in Chancery, for the Plaintiff to have an Injunction, to quit his Possession till the hearing of the Cause; this, or any other such Order not being final, is Interlocutory, INTERMISSION Febrium: See Apyrexia.

intermittensmorbus.c: INTERMITTENS Morbus, is a Disease which comes at certain times, and then remits a little.

internodiuminbotany.c: INTERNODIUM, in Botany, is the Space con - tained between any two Knots or Joints of the Stalk of a Plant. !

internusanris.c: INTERNUS Anris, is a Muscle which lies in a Bony Channel evacuated in the Os Petrofum, which makes one of the Pariete ) Timpani: One part of this Channel is without the Tympanum, and lies in the upper part of the Bony Passage which goes from the Ear to the Palate; the other part, which is within the Tympanum, advancing as far as the Fene - star Oval is, ' makes jin that place a riling, upon which, as on a Pulley, the Tendon of this Muscle passes to the other Side of the Tympanum, and. n [ et it self at the posterior part of the Handle of the Mal - leus, a little below the Insertion of the External Muf - cle, by which means it draws towards the Os Petro - sum. When this Muscle ads, it pulls the Manubri - um of the Malleus towards the Os Petrofum, where - by the Membrana Tympafii become some what con - cave outwardly;

interosseimanus.c: INTEROSSEI Manus, are the Muscles of the Fingers, which are diftingmfhed into External and Internal j they are aptly so named from their Situa - tions. Authors disagree in their Number, some rec - koning fix, others eight, amongst which they e - iteemthe AbduBor Minimi Digits, and Indicts -, but Mr. Cowper inclines to the first Opinion, conceiving the two latter named Muscles do not deserve these Denominations. They arise FIelhy internally in the Palm from the superior parts of the Metacarpal Bones next the Carpus, whence descending, they become Tendinous at the first Internode of each Finger laterally, and pass to their Ihfertions with the Extensor Digit or um Communis -, each interstice of the Metacarpal Bones entertaining tWO Muscles inserted to the Sides, of the Fingers. When all these Interossei ad together, they draw the Fingers near each other, and assist in their Extension, as Ga - len takes notice; at which time they, together with the AbduBor Indicis, and Minimi Digits, are Capa - ble of divaricating the Fingers, which Adion can - not be performed without some Difficulty by them when they are bended; which Contrivance of the Most Wife Archited is also observed by Galen.

interosseipedis.c: INTEROSSEI Pedis, are Muscles of the Foot they are reckoned to be seven in Number. They de - rive their Names from their Situation, and may each deserve a proper Appellation from their Use. The First may be called AbduBor Minimi Digits. The Second, which is the largest, draws the next Toe towards the lesser, and may be called, AbduBor Auricularius. The Third antagonists the former, and is an Ah duBor of the Toe. The Fourth may be called Abductor Medii DU gits The Fifth is an AbduBor of the lame. The Sixth is an AbduBor j and Seventh, AbduBor Indijcss Pedis. All these arise Fleshy from the superior part of the OJfa Metatarsi of the lesser Toes, and becoming bel - lied, grow Tendinous at their Insertions to the first Internode of each lesser Toe laterally.

interrogation.c: INTERROGATION, is aFigurein Rhetorickf in which the Passion of the Speaker introduces a thing by way of Question, to make its Truth the more conspicuously appear.

interruption.c: INTERRUPTION, as some call ir, is the lame with Disjundion of Proportion in Geometry, and is noted thus, (:: ) and signifieth the breaking off of the Ratio in the Middle of four disjund or diE crete Proportionals, As A: B:: C: D j that is. As A is to B:: So is C to D.

interscapularia.c: INTERSCAPULARIA, are the Cavities be - twixt the Shoulder - blades and the Vertebres.

intersectioninmathematicks.c: INTERSECTION, in Mathematicks, fignifi. es the cutting of one Line or Plane by another: Thus we fay, that the mutual InterfeBion of two Planes, is a Right Line.

interspinalescolli.c: INTERSPIN ALES Colli these are small fieldy Muscles of the Neck, arising from the superior parts of each double spinal Process of the Neck, except of the second Vertebra; and are inferred to the in - senior Parts of all the said double Spines. When these Muscles ad, they draw the Spines of the Vertebra of the Neck nearer each other. These were first discovered in the Year.

interstellaraword.c: INTERSTELLAR, a Word used by some Au - thors, to express those parts of the Universe that are without and beyond our Solar System; arid which are supposed as Planetary System moving round each fix ’ d Status the Center, of their Motion, as the Sun is of ours.: And if it be true, - as tis not improbable. That each fix ’ d Star may thus be a Sun to feme habitable Orbs, that may move round: lit, the Interftcllar World will be infinitely the greater part of ttheUni verse. r

intertigoorattritus.c: INTERTIGO, or Attritus, is cutting or fretting the Cuticula off of the parts near the Fundament, or betwixt the Thighs.

interval.c: INTER VAL, in Mulick, is the Distance or Dis - ference between any two Sounds, whereof one is more Grave, and the other more Acute. They make several Divisions of an Interval, as first into Simple X A Compound The Simple Intervals are the OBave, and all that are within it, as the Second ? Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh, with their Varieties: The Compound ones are all those that are greater than an OBave, as the Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, &c. with their Varieties. An Interval is also divided into Just or True, and mo False: All the above - mention'd Intervals, with their ' I N V N W m their Varieties, whether Major or Minor are JuH but the diminutive, or superfluous ones are all False See O anams DiEt. Matth. P.. An Interval is also divided into a Conjonance and a Dijfonance which fee.

INTERVAL of the Fits of easie Reflexion, and of easie Tranfmillion of the Rays of Light, is the Spaces between every Return of the Fit and the next Return. These Intervals Sir If. Newton shews how to colled, and thence to determine whether the Rays shall be reflected or transmitted at their subst - quent Incidence on any pellucid Medium. ( See Light, Gc. and Newtons Opticks, Book a. Part. )

intestatesinlaw.c: INTESTATES, in Law, there are two kinds of Intejlates, one that makes no Will at all another that makes a Will, and nominates Executors, but they refuse in which he dies as an Intedate, and the Ordinary commits Adniiniftration.

intrusion.c: INTRUSION, is when the Ancestor dies seized of any Estate of Inheritance, expectant upon an fi - ate for Life and then the Tenant for Life dies, between whose Death, and the Entry of the Heir, a Stranger does interpose and intrude.

intrusione.c: INTRUSIONE, is a Writ that lies against the Intruder.

intuition.c: INTUITION, according to Mr. Lock., is the Perception of the certain Agreement or Disagree - ments any two Idea ’ s immediately compared to - gether.

invidiatusinlaw.c: INVIDIATUS, in Law, is when one has been accused of some Crime, which being not fully pro - ved, he is put fub debit a side juffione, i. e. Suretijhip.

invectedaterminheraldry.c: INVECTED, a Term in Heraldry, signifying diredfly contrary to Engrailed; which fee.

inventory.c: INVENTORY, is the Description or Repertory orderly made of all Dead Men ’ s Goods and Chat - tels, prized by four or more Credible Men, which every Executor or Administrator is bound to exi - bit to the Ordinary at such times as he shall ap - point.

inverseproportion.c: INVERSE Proportion, or Proportion by Inversion: See the Word Proportion, N..

invoice.c: INVOICE, is a Particular of the Value, Cu - stom, and Charges of any Goods sent by a Mer - chant in another Man ’ s Ship, and consigned to a Fadtor. IN V OLU CRU M Cordis: See Pericardium.
INVOICE, iz Car. z. c. is a Particular ofthe Value, Custom and Charges of any Goods lent by a Merchant in another Man ’ s Ship, and Consign ’ d to a Fadlor or Correspondent in ano - ther Country.
