ionickorderofarchitecture.c: IONICK Order of Architecture, is the Form of a Column or Pillar invented by the lonians in Ancient Greece, by way of Improvement of the Beauty of the Dorici Order: Which as it was taken from the Figure of a Robust Man ’ s Body, and designed to represent Solidity and Strength; so the Ionium ha - ving more regard to Beauty, chose an Order of a more Elegant Proportion, which occasioned this Order to be called, The Feminine Order, and soon after it sprung up that of the Caryatides. The Promotions of this Pillar, as they are taken from the Famous one in the Temple of Fortuna Vi - rulis at Rome, now the Church of St. Mary the E - egyptian, are these; The entire Order from the Superficies of the Area to the Cornice, are Modules or Diameters. The Column with its Base and Capital, contains Modules. The Entablature ( i: e. the Architrave, Freife and Cornice ) contain four Modules. The Valuta of the Capital, is of an Oval Form, TheColumns in this Order are often hollow ’ d and furrow'd with Gutters; and sometimes ’ tis done only to the third part of the Column, reckoning from the Bottom; and then that third part hath its Gut - ters filled with little Rods or Battoons, all the part of the hollow above being left empty.

jonthusorvarus.c: JONTHUS, or Varus, is a little, hard, callous Swelling in the Skin of the Face. Blanchard.

journeysaccounts.c: JOURNEYS Accounts, is a Term in Law, to be thus understood: If a Writ be abated without the Default of the Plaintiff or Demandant, he may purchase a new Writ, which if it be purchased by Journeys Accounts j ( that is, within as little time as he possibly can after the Abatement of the first Writ ) then this second Writ shall be as a Continuance of the first, and so shall ought the Tenant or Defendant of his Voucher, Plea, or Non tenure, Joint - tenant cy fully administred, ( c. or any other Plea which arises upon Matter happening after the Date of the first Writ; and fifteen Days have been held a con - lenient Time for the purchase of the new Writ.

joy.c: JOY, is a Delight of the Mind, from the Confi - duration of the present, or assured approaching Pos - session of a Good; and we are then possessed of a - ny Good, when we have it so in our power that we can use it when we please.

jointure.c: JOINTURE, is a Covenant, whereby the Hus - band, or some other Friend in his bejialf, affureth unto his Wife, in respect of Marriage, Lands or Tenements for a Term of Life: Or other wife It is so called, either because granted Eat i one junRura in Matrimonio; or because the Land in Fran t - marry age is given jointly to the Husband and Wife, and after to the Heirs of their Bodies, where - by the Husband and Wife be made Joint - Tenants during the Coverture.

iris.c: IRIS, is that Fibrous Circle next to the Pupil of the Eye, distinguished with Variety of Colours: See Vvea Membrana. ’ Tis so called from its Semi - litude to a Rainbow, fin Latin Iris. ) Also those changeable Colours which sometimes appear in the Glasses of Telescopes, Microscopes, ( c. are called Iris for the fame Reason; as is that coloured SpeRrum, which a Triangular Prifma - tick Glass, will project on a Wall, when placed ( at a due Angle ) in the Sun - Beams: See Bain - bow.

irony.c: IRONY, is a Trope in Rhetorick, by which we speak contrary to our Thoughts; as to fay. Such a me is a very honest Man, when we know he is not - rioufiy Corrupt.

iron.c: IRON - SICK, a Ship or a Boat is said to be Iron - ficli, when her Spikes are so eaten with Rust or Nails, and so worn away, that they make Hollows in the Planks, whereby the Ship leaks.

IRON. In the Forest of Dean in Gloucefler - Jhire the best Iron Oar is of a Bluish Colour, and is called Brujh Oar: But. this being melted alone produces a;. Metal very short and brittle: To remedy which Inconvenience, they makeule ( Cynder, which is found in great Quantity where any old Works have been in that County: For in former Times their Bellows being moved only by Hand, their Furnaces produced a Fire much less intense, than those they now employ: So that formerly they melted down only the Prin - cial Part of the Oar, rejecting the reft as useless. This Refuse is the Cynder; which being mingled with the Oar in a due, Quantity, gives it that ex - cellent Temper of Toughness, for which this Iron is preferred before any brought from Abord. The Oar is first Calcined in Kilns, like ord - nary Lime - Kilns, which they fill up to the Top with Coal and Oar, SSS. Then putting Fire to the Bottom, they let it burn till the Coal be wafted. This is done without Fiijion of the Me - tal, and serves to consume the more drossy Part of the Oar, and to make it friable. From hence they carry it to the Furnaces, which are built of Brick or Stone, about Foot fguare on the Outside, R O I R O Outside, and near Foot in Height. Within they are not above or Foot over in the Mid - dle, and the Top and Bottom have a yet narrower compass; so they are almost of the shape of an Egg. Behind the Furnace are placed two very large Pair of Bellows, whose Nofes meet at a little Hole near the Bottom. These are compress - fed together by certain Buttons placed on the Axis, of a very large Overjhot Wheel. The Furnaces are at first filled with Oar and Cynder, intermix ’ d with Fuel, which in these Works is always of Charcoal, laying them hol - low at the Bottom, that they may the more east - ly take Fire. But after they are once kindled the Materials run together into a hard Cake or Lump, which isfuftain ’ d by the Fashion of the Furnace; and through this the Metal, as it melts, trickles down into the Receivers, where there is a Passage open, by which they clear away the Scum and Dross. Before this lies a great Bed of Sand, where - in they make Furrows of what fashion they please, into which they let their Metal; which is made so very fluent by the Violence of the Fire, that it continues boiling for a good while. The Fur - naces are kept at work Day and Night for many Months, still supplying the Waste of the Vue, and other Materials with fresh pour ’ d in at the Top. From these Furnaces they bring their Sows and Pigs of Iron ( as they call them ) to their Forges. These Forges are of two forts, tho ' ( landing toge - ther under the fame Roof: And one they call Finery, the other their Chafery. Both of them are on Hearths, on which they place great Heaps of Sea - Coal, and behind them Bellows, like the for - mer, but not near so large. Into their Finery they first put the Pigs of Iron, placing three or four of them together behind the Fire, with a little of one End thrust into it; where foftning by de - grees, they stir and work them with long Bars of Iron, ' till the Metal runs together into a round Mass or Lump; which they call an Half Bloom. This they take out, and giving it a few Strokes with their Sledges, they carry it tb a great weighty Hammer, raised by the Motion of a Wa - ter - Wheel; where applying it dextrously to the Blows, they presently beat it out into a thick short Square: This they put into the Finery again; and heating it red hot they work it out under the fame Hammer till it comes to be in the slape of a Bar in the Middle, but with two square Knobs on the Ends. Last of all they give it other Heats in the Chafery, and more Workings under the Hammer, till they have brought their Iron into Bars of several Shapes and Sizes. If they omit any one Process, it will be furcto want something of its Toughness, which they esteem its Perfection. For the Backs of Chimneys, Hearths of O vens, or the like, they take the melted Metal out of the Receivers in great Ladles, and pour it into Moulds of fine Sand: Philof. Trans. N.. At Milthorpe in Lancajhire they have several forts of Iron - Stone, feme of it making Coldjhire - Iron; that is, such as is brittle when it is cold. Another Fort makes Fed / hire, which is such as is apt to break if it be hammer ’ d when ’ tisof a dark Red Heat; and therefore they are never melted down but in Mixture, and so they yield an india - ferent good fort of Iron.. They have of late made it much better than before, by melting the Sow - Metal over again, as likewise by using Turf and Charcoal; whereas formerly the Fuel was only Charcoal. They first burn the Iron - Stone, and then for e - very leyenteen Baskets of this burnt Stone they put in one of Lime - Stone unburnt, to make it melt freely and cast the Cynder, which they al - ways take off from the melted front before they let it run. The Bottom of the Furnace is about two Yards square, and so rises perpendicularly for a Yard or more, which is also lined within with a Wall of the best Fire - Stone, to keep off the Force of the Fire from the Walls of the Furnace. The Bellows which are very large, and moved by Water, enter about the middle of the Focus. - The reft of theFurnace is raised above this fix or fevers Yards fpuare - wife, but tapering; so that the top Hole where they throw in the Mine and Fuel, is but half a Yard square. When they find it to have subside about a yard and quarter, they fill the Furnace again. Their Forge is much like that of a common Blacksmith ’ s, about one yard and half over, and of the fame height. The Hearth is all of Sovp Iron, much of the slape of a Broad - brim ’ d Hat, with the Crown downwards. The hollow place the fill and heap up with Charcoal, and lay the Oar ( first broken into pieces as big as a Pigeon ’ s Egg ) all round about the Charcoal on the flat Hearth, to bake it, as it were, or neal it; thrust - ing it by little and little into the Hollow, and keep blowing for twelve Hours. Then they pull out a Stopple at the Bottom of the Wall, and out comes all the Glaffie Cynder, being very liquid, leaving the Iron, which is never in a perfedl Fusion, in a Lump at the Bottom: This they take out with great Tongs, and, turn it under heavy Hammers moved by Water, which at the fame time beat off, or rather squeeze out the fluid - Scoria: or Dross, and after several Heats form it into Bars ! ' They use no Lime - Stone, or any thing else to promote the Flux. The get about x Pound Weight of Metal at one Melting, out of about three times as much Oar. The Iron Mine in Sujfexlies from four Foot deep to forty and upwards. There are several forts of Mine, feme hard, feme gentle, feme rich, feme poor, feme fine, feme courser. The Iron Masters mix different forts of Mine together, otherwise it will not melt to so good an Advantage. When the Mine is brought in they take Small - coal, and lay a Row of that and a Row of Mine alternately, S. S. S. one above another; and fet - ting the Coals on Fire, therewith burn the Oar: This is done to J mollifier it, that so it may be broken in small pieces, otherwise it would not mslt in the Furnace, but come away whole: Nor must it be over - burnt, for then it will: top, as they call it; - that is, run together in a Mass. After it is burnt ’ cis beat into small pieces with an Iron Sledge, and then put into the Furnace, which is before charged with Coals, on the Top of which it is call, where it melts and falls down into the Hearth in about twelve Hours more or less, and then ’ tisrun into a Sow. This Hearth is made of Sand - Stone, as also its Sides round to the height of about a yard; and then the reft of the Furnace is lined up. to the top with Brick. When they. begin upon a new Furnace, they put Fire for a day or two before they begin to blow: Then they blow gently, and increase by I degrees, till they come to csse heightirt ten Weeks or more. Every I R O Every fix days they call a Foundry, in which time they make Tun of Iron: That is, if you divide the whole Sum of Iron they make by the Foundky - or at fir ft they make less in a Foundry, at last more. The Hearth, by the force of the Fire continual - ly blown, grows wider and wider; so that if at first it contains so much as will make a Sow of or Pound Weight; at last it will con - tain so much as will make a Sow of Pound. The lejfifer pieces of Pound and under, they call Pigs. Of twenty four Load of Coals, they expect eight Tun of Sow. To every Load of Coals, which consists of eleven Quarters, they put a Load of Mine, containing eighteen Bufhels. A Hearth, if made of good Stone, will ord - warily last forty Foundays or Weeks: During which time the Fire is never let go out. They never blow twice on one Hearth, tho ’ they go upon it but five or fix Foundays. The Cynder, like Scum, Twigs upon the melted Metal in the Hearth, and is let out once or twice before a Sow is cast. The Manner of hVorlfng Iron at the Forge or Flatnmer, ' In every Forge there are t, wo Fires at least, which, as before is observed, are called, one the Finery, and the other the Chafery. At the Finery, by the Working of the Hammer, they bring it into Blooms and Anconies, thus: They roll the Sow at first into the Fire, and then melt off a piece of about f of a Hundred Pound Weight; which, as soon as ’ tis broken off, they call a Loop. This Loop they take out with their Shingling - Tongs, and beat it with Iron Sledges on an Iron Plate near the Fire; that so it may not fall in pieces, but be in a capacity to be carried under the Hammer; where it is beat very gently at first, only to draw Cynders and Dross out of the Matter: But afterwards they let out or draw more Water, and so by degrees beat it thicker and stronger, till they bring it to a Bloom; which is a four - square Mass, about two Foot long. This Operation they call Shingling the Loop. This done, they immediately return it to the Finery a - gain; and after two or three Heats, and Work - ing, they bring it to an Ancony; whole Figure is in the middle a Bar of about three Foot long, and of the shape they intend the whole Bar shall be made of; but at both ends is a square piece'left rough, to be wrought at the Chafery. Note, At the Finery, three Load of the biggest Coals go to the making of one Tun of Iron. At the Chafery they only draw out the two Ends suitable to what was drawn out at the Fi - very in the Middle, and so finish the Bar. Note, One Load of smaller Coals draws out a Tun of Iron at the Chafery. At the Finery, they expect that one Man and a Boy should make two Tun of Iron in a Week; and at the Chafery, that two Men would take up, that is, ' Make or Work five or fix Tun in a Week. One thing is, remarkable here: They fay, That if into the Hearth where they work the Iron Sows ( whether the Finery or the Chafery ) you cast on the Iron a piece of Brass, it will hinder the Metal from Working, causing it to spatter about ] U B so, that it cannot. be wrought into a solid piece - Bays - GoBeB. of. irradiation.c: IRRADIATION, is a Word used by Van HeL mont, and some other Chymifts, to express the O - operation of some Mineral Medicines, which they will have to impart their Vertue, without emitting any thing Material or Substantial out of them, or without the Emanation of any Corporeal Effluvia. Thus, for Instance, They tell you that some Am timonial Preparations, as its Glass and Crocus Metal - lorum, will give an Emetick Quality to Wine, ( c. without any manner of Diminution of its Weight; But it doth not appear that they were well enough exercised in Statical Experiments, either to have nice Scales, or to know how to use them, and there - fore, doubtleis, do too boldly call that Diminution which was only not so sensibly so to them i Buthow a Body should communicate its Vomitive Quality to a Liquor, without impregnating it with some of its fine and subtle Emetick Particles, is hardly poise - ble to conceive.

irregularbodies.c: IRREGULAR Bodies, are Solids which are not ? terminated by equal and like Surfaces.

issuantaterminheraldry.c: ISSUANT, a Term in Heraldry, when a Lion, or other Be ait, is drawn in a Coat of Arms, just if - suing out of the Bottom Line of any Chief, Sense,. &c. but if it come out of the Middle of any Ordi - nary, they call it Naiffaht; that is, Nascent, just Coming out as it were from the Womb.

issueatermincommonlaw.h: ISSUE a Term in Common Law
issueatermincommonlaw.c: ISSUE, a Term in Common Law, having di - vers Applications; sometimes tis taken for the Children begotten between a Man and his Wife j sometimes from Profits growing from Amerciaments hr Fines; and sometimes from Profits of Lands or Tenements; sometimes for that Point of Matter depending in Suit, whereupon the Parties join, and ptit their Cause to the Trial of the Jury: And yet in all these it hath but one Signification, which is an Effect of a Cause proceeding, as the Children be the Effedf of the Marriage between the Parents: The Profits growing to the King or Lord, from the Punishment of any Man's Offence, is the EffeCt ot his TranfgrefTton: The Point referred to the Trial of Twelve Men is the EffeCt of Pleading or Pro - cels, Issue in this last Signification, is either General or Special. General Issue, seemeth to be that Whereby it is re - served to the Jury to bring in their Verdidt, whether the Defendant hath done any such thing as the Plaintiff layeth to his Charge. f For Example i If it be an Offence against any Statute, and the Defendant plead, Not Guilty; this being put to the Jury, is called, The General Issue. And if a Man complain of a private Wrong which the Defendant deniet - h, and pleads no Wrong nor Disseisin, and if this be referred to the Jury, it is likewise the General IJfke. he Special Issue then must be that, when Special Matters being alledged by the Defendant in his De - fence, both Parties join thereupon, and fb grow ra - ther to a Demurrer, if it - be question juris, or to Trial by the Jury, if it be quejliofabli.

isthmusingeography.c: ISTHMUS, in Geography, is a little Neck or Part of Land joining a Peninsula to the Continent.

isthmusinanatomy.c: ISTHMUS, in Anatomy, according to some, is that Part which lies betwixt the Mouth and the Gullet, like a Neck of Land j also the Ridge that separates the Nostrils.

itenerarium.c: ITENERARIUM, is a Chyrurgeon ’ s Instrument, which being fixed in the Urinary Passage, shews the Neck or SphinCter of the Bladder, that an Incifi - on may be more surely made to find out the Stone: " Tis usually thrust up through the Cavity of a Fi - ftulous Catheter, which saves it from wounding the Urethra as it goes.

jubabotanick.c: JUB a Botanick. Word, signifying a soft loose Beard, which hangs at the Ends of the Husks of some Plants of the Frumentaceom, Kind; as particularly in Millet.

judgeandjudges.c: JUDGE and Judges, have all their Commissions bounded with this Limitation, Faduri quodadjuftiti - arn pertinent fecundum legem & confuetudinum An - glia;. The Judge at his Creation takes this Hath, That he shall indifferently minister Justice to all “ them that shall have any Suit or Plea before him ie and this he shall not forbear to do,, though the King by his Letters, or by express Word b Mouth, should command the contrary, &c JUDGMENT, in Law, is the Censure of the Judges lo called, and is the very Voice and Final. Doom of the Law, and therefore is always taken for unquestionable Truth. Of Judgments, some are Final, and some not Ft - nal: See Coke and Littleton, Fcl.. - JUDGMENT Mr. Lock, defines to be a Faculty of separating carefully one from another, those Ideas wherein any, even theleaft Difference can be found, thereby to avoid being mislead by Similitude and by Affinity, to take one thing for another. Others define it to be that Action of the Mind by which assembling together several Ideas, we ei - ther deny or affirm This to be That. Thus, considering the Idea of the Earth, and the Idea of Roundness, we affirm or deny the Earth to be round.

jugular.c: JUGULAR - VEINS, are thole Veins winch goes towards the Skull by the Neck; and are of two forts, vt. External and Internal. The External Jugulars ascend on the Outside of the Neck, and are usually open ’ d where one is let Blood in that Part for any Distemper in the Head, Quiufey, &c. The Internal Jugulars arise from the Subclavian ', by the Sides of the Wind - pipe, and palling along the Skull in two. Branches, are dispersed through the Dura Mater, &c.

jalap.c: JALAP, from the Greek eieria, or, as some fay ? from the Perfick Word Julcb, which signifies a Sweet Portion, is a grateful Medicine composed of Distilled Waters, Spirits, &c. and sweetened to the Patient ’ s Palate with Sugar, or some agreeable Syrup.

JULIAN - PERIOD, is a Cycle of Confer cutive Years, produced by the contiriual Multiplica - tion of the three Cycles vis. Th tt of the Sun of Years, that of the Moon of Years, and that of the Indi & ion of Years; so that this Epocha, al - though but Artificial or Feign ’ d, ( and which was the Invention of the Famous Julius Scaliger ) is yet of very good Use, in that every Year within the Period, is distinguishable by a certain peculiar Cha - rater; for the Year of the Sun, Moon, and Indic - tion will not be the fame again, till the whole Years be revolved: Scaliger fix ’ d the Beginning of this Period Years before the Creation. For the finding the Tear of the Julian Period, you have this Ifule: Multiply the Solar Cycle by, the Lunar bj,, and the IndiBion by Then divide the Sum of Products by, and the Remainder of the Division ( without having re - gard to the Quotient ) shall be the Year required after. julus.c: JULUS, is a Botanick Word for thole Catalim, as some call them, or long Worm - like Tufts, or Palms, as they are called in Willows, which at the Beginning of the Year grow out of, and hang pen - dulous down from Hazels, Wallnut - Trees, &c. The Accurate Mr. I ( ay thinks them to be a kind of Collection of the Stamina of the Flowers of the Tree because in Fertile Trees and Plants they have abundance of Seminal Vessels or Seed - Pods.

jupiter.c: JUPITER: The Proportion of Jupiter to our Earth, is about to. The Periodical Time of Jupiter s Revolution a - bout the Sun, is in the Space of Years, or Days; and he revolves round his Axis in the Space of o Hours; which very swift Motion may cause that Excess of his Equatorial Diameter above his Polar, which you will find below j whereas in the Sun and Moon which take, the one, the other Days in their Revolution round their Axis, there is no such Inequality between their Polar and Equa - trial Diameters observed. The Mean Distance of Jupiter from the Sun, ac - cording to I kepler; to Bullialdus according to the Periodical Time of its Revolution: Such Parts of which the Mean Distance between the Earth and Sun is that is, a - bout English Miles. According to Mr. Caffini, Jupiter's greatest Di - stance from the Earth is - - his mean Di - stance; and least Distance Semi - diameters of the Earth. And the Diameter of Jupiter is equal to and a Half Semi - diameters of the Earth. Wherefore the Globe of Jupiter must be greater than that of the Earth by times. The Semi - diameter of Jupiter, seen from the Sun, is but Seconds, In the Year, Campani ( by the help of an excellent Telescope ) observed certain Protube - rances and Inequalities in the Surface ot this Pla - net. He fa V also in his Body the Shrdows of his Sa - tellites, and followed them with his Eye till hefaw them go off the Disk. In the fame Year, May the th, Hours, P. M. Mr, Hook, with a Telescope of Foot, observed; a small Spot in the biggest of the three obscure Belts of Jupiter and within two Hours after he found that the said Spot had moved from Eaftto Weft about half the Length of the Diameter of Jupiter. Mr. Caffini observed also, near the fame Time, a permanent Spot in the Disk of Jupiter; by whose help he not only found that Jupiter turns about up - on his own Axis, but also the Time of such Con - version, which he estimates to be Hours, and Minutes. Which was also confirmed by better Obfervati - ons of a Spot in the Year The Equatorial Diameter of Jupiter to his Po - lar one, Sir If. Newton computes to be as f to f. Captain Halley, in his Preface to his Catalogue of the Southern Stars, faith, That he found Jupiter to move swifter than he is supposed to do by the Aftrononxical Tables. The fame Learned Person thinks, That the Rea - fon of the Error ( of about or Minutes in Time ) i the Tables in calculating the Eclipses of the Sa - tellites, arises from some ( mail Excentficity in the Motion of the Planet, and from the Oval Figure of his Body newly mentioned, whose quick Rota - tion round his Axis by the Vis Centifuga, dilates his Equinoctial Parts, and makes his Meridians much Elliptical, so as to be discernible by the Telescope. The Sun ’ s Heat in Jupiter, is at most not above one twenty fifth part of what it is with us and consequently Would be very uncomfortable living there ( if at all possible ) for Men of our Confuta - tion; and yet some are very fond of thinking Jupi ter an excellent Place to live in. The Distance of Jupiter from the Sun, is above five times as great as that of the Earth from the Sun, ( fee Gregorys Aftron. ) and consequently the Dia - meter of the Sun to any Eye in Jupiter, will be not a fifth part of what it appears to us, and therefore his Disk will be above times less, and in the fame Proportion will his Light and Heat be. The Artificial Day and Night ( each of Hours ) is of the fame length in Jupiter all over his Surface j because the Axis of his Diurnal Revolution, is near - ly at Right Angles to the Plane of his Annual Or - bit round the Sun, Although Jupiter hath four Primary Planets be - low him; yet an Eye placed there, and of no har - per Sight than one of ours, could never behold any one ot them, unless as Spots tranfiting over the Sun ’ s Disk when they happen to be between the Jo vial Eye and the Sun: Eor Mars, which goes fur theft of all from the Sun, will not in Jupiter be seen above Degrees from him and since that Planet is but small, and refletfts but a weak Light, so near the Sun it cannot be visible: So that Saturnis the on - ly Planet that can be seen in Jupiter, except his own four Moons or Satellites. The Sun ’ s Parallax seen from Jupiter, will scarce be sensible any more than Saturn s neither being much above Seconds so that the Sun ’ s app - rent Diameter in Jupiter will not be above Mi - nutes: But the outermost of his Satellites will ap - pear almost as great as the Moon doth to us; vi. of five times the Diameter, and times the Disk of the Sun, seen from the fame Planet; and if rhe other Satellites are not less than the outermost, they will yet appear much greater, ( and the Learned Mr. Hugens conceives them not much less than our Earth ) and gives the Planet a good Light in the Nights, which also can never there be very long. Dr. Gregory, ( from whence this comparative A - astronomy is colle & ed ) faith also, That an Aftroi comer placed in Jupiter, would easily compare die Distances of the four inferior Planets with the Diameters of Jupiter, as we do the Distances of us from the Planets, by comparing them with the Diameter of the Earth: And this would be done as to the four nearest ones, easier than we compute the Distance of the Moon by the Earths Diame - ter for the Horizontal Parallax of the remotest of the Planets seen from Jupiter, is above twice as great as the Horizontal Parallax of the Moon seen from the Earth, and therefore muff: be very sense - ble and considerable. And tho ’ the Globe of Ju pitch be vastly large, in comparison of our Earth yet the Suns Parallax, when he ’ s beheld from Jupi - ter, will not be quite Seconds, and Consequent ly scarce sensible: Nor will the Parallax of a turn, ( though when in Opposition to the Sun, and next to Jupiter ) be much greater; and therefore ’ twill be Very difficult for the Jovial Astronomer to estimate the Distance of Saturn, of of the Sun, from that Planer. P g g i ( S Indeed if he can dis cover that Jupiter moves round the Sun, he may be able ( as the Docftor shews, Prop.. ) to determine the Ratio of the Di - stance of Jupiter and Saturn from the Sun, other - wile not. Our Jovial Ajironomer therefore by the help of his Senses, would distinguish two kinds of Planets; Four nearer to him, which are the Satellites, and two ( as the Sun and Saturn ) more remote; and these latter would appear with a lester Diameter, the former with a greater: Of the remotest, the Sun would appear in a Diameter about fix Minutes, but the Diameter of Saturn would scarce be of a Minute. Of the four nearer Planets or Satellites, the Fourth would appear to an Eye in Jupiter of the Bigness the Moon doth to us; that is, with a Dia meter five times greater, and a Disk twenty five times greater than the Sun doth there: Besides, the four nearer, and apparently greater ones, will be di - ftinguifhed from the more remote and lesser ones, in this, That in the nearer Planets, the Squares of the Periodick Times, are as the Cubes of their Di - stances from the Center of Jupiter; which would by no means be true, if any one of the greater were compared with any one of the lesser. And although the nearer these Planets are, they appear the greater; yet the Sun will be immensely more bright than they; for from their Faces, which depend up - on their Situation, with respect to the Sun, they will appear like so many Moons: From whence a Spe & tor in Jupiter will have four kinds of Months, according to the Number of Moons. There will be contained above of the least Months in a Year, and about half the Number of Months next to these: The Number of the Months of the third Satellite contain ’ d in a Year, will be nearly subdue - ple of the second, or subquadruple of the first; and the Months of the greatest will be about: S that although the Notation of Time be much more intricate in Jupiter, by reason of the great Number of Days which their Year contains; yet it is much facilitated by these four kinds of Months; for in the least Month there are only Days and a Quarter, but in the greatest something more than. Besides, these Moons suffer an Eclipse when they, being in Opposition to the Sun, happen to fall into the Shadow of Jupiter; and again, when they, ( be - ing in Conjunction with the Sun, projects their Sha - dows to Jupiter, they make an Eclipse of the Sun to an Eye placed in that Region ot Jupiter, where the Shadow falls ( which Region is a very small part: of Jupiter's Surface ) just as our Moon does: But because the Orbits of thole Moons about Jupiter, are in a Plane which is inclined to, or makes an Angle with Jupiter's Orbit about the Sun, and are all of them nearly in the fame Plane, excepting the second, which deviates a little upon this Account, I lay, their Ecliples are Central, and consequently most lasting, when the Sun is in one of the Nodes of those Moons: But when the Sun is put of this Position, the Eclipses may be Total, though not Cen - tral, because the Breadth of Jupiter s Shadow, is nearly decuple the Breadth of any of the Satellites; and the apparent Diameter of any of those Moons, is nearly quintuple the apparentDiameter of the Sun. And this remarkable Inequality of the Diameters, and the small Inclination the Plane of the Orbits of the Satellites has to the Plane of Jupiter s Orbit found the Sun, is the Reason why in each Revolu - tion there happens Eclipses both of the Satellites and of the Sun, though the Sun be at a eonfidera -, J u R ble Distance from the Nodes: And the inferior of these Satellites, though the Sun to a Spectator in Jupiter, be at his greatest Distance from their Nodes, -, are nevertheless Eclipsed, and Eclipse the Sun; but the remotest of them in this Case, for two Years together, escapes falling into Jupiter's Shadow, and Jupiter into its Shadow; and the Phenomena of partial Eclipses in the intermediate Times and Pla - ces, will be apparent to a Spedator in Jupiter. Far - ther, it sometimes happens here that one Moon E eclipses another, whose Phasis is sometimes very dis - ferent, nay contrary to the Eclipse of a Moor., say ling into the Shadow of Jupiter, which was deYcri - bed above; for in this the Oriental Limb is first dar - kened, and the Occidental Limb emerges last; but in others of them the Occidental Limb is first dar - kened, and the Oriental Limb emerges last; and in others contrarily. The Shadow of Jupiter, though it go far beyond its Satellites, yet does not reach any other Planet; as the Shadow of all other primary Planets do; for no other Planet, except Saturn, could beimmerged in it, tho ’ it was infinite; but the Shadow of Jupi - ter cannot reach Saturn, except the Diameter of Jupiter were half the Diameter of the Sun, and ir is scarce - of it. If the Surfaceof Jupiter were chiefly Water, and we suppose the Seas there to be Navigable, the Sai - lors would have great Advantages, as well because the Nights are very short, and very light from the Numbers of their Moons; as because these Moons would be of singular use to ’ em in directing their Courses. For from those manifold Eclipses the Longitude of a Place would be easily determined, and Hydro - graphical Tables accurately constructed, which is very Advantagious in so vast a Globe as that of Ju - peter whose Surface being Centuple, ( nay, accord - ding to Hugens, times as much ) the Surface of the Earth would render its Mensuration very labo - rious: But the Flux and Reflux of the Sea, occ - sion ’ d by these four Moons, ( for the Force of the Sun would be very little there ) would be very dis - ferent, and besides, would be very difficultly brought to a Calculation. r

JUPITER. The Calculation of the Eclipses of Jupiter s Satellites being a thing of great Use for determining the Longitude of Places on the Earth; I judge ’ d it necessary to insert the Man - ner and Method of it here from Mr. Whifions Pral eel i ones Astronomic, p,. He takes for an Example an Eclipse of the first Satellite; because, both those Excellent Aftrono - mers, CaJJini and Halley have ihewn how to Cal - oculate that by proper T ables; and that the fame Method will serve to find the Eclipses of the o - ther Satellites of this Planet. And he observes that these Caffmian Tables are formed after a new and accurate Method, and will give the Moment of the Eclipses in as new and accurate a Way. It is supposed there, That the Periodick Time of this first Satellite precisely one th Part of the Periodick Time of Jupiter, from one A - aphelion to another. Whence the Equations of the Jovial Orbit being turn ’ d in Minutesof Time, and adapted to those particular Revolutions of the Satellites, will make good the principal Parts of the Equation of these Eclipses. ' Tis to be ob - served also, that these Tables suppose the Aphe - lion of Jupiter to be in the Beginning of the th Degree of Libra; and that the Orbit of the Sa - stellite is so little distant from the Plane of the Orbit of Jupiter, or also of the Ecliptick; that the Differences thence arising may usually not be taken notice of. Note also, That in the acc - rate Calculation of these Eclipses, there is need ol another Equation, according to the various Position of the Earth to Jupiter. Which R. eftitu - tion of the Position, suppose the Opposition of the SC ? rand Jupiter, contains f Periods of this Sa - stellite. The first Observer of this Equation, Mr. Ro - mer, asserts, That ’ tis in its greatest Quantity Minutes of Time; but CaJJini faith it don ’ t exceed Minutes and o Seconds. The Caule of this Equation is the successive Propagation or Motion of Light; which is by no means instant - taneous. And from this Fountain the Equations of the - f - Revolutions of the second Satellite, being respectively adapted, do compleat the fe - cond Parts of these Eclipses. But a little Table may also be added, shewing the Half - Stay of the Satellite in the Shadow of Jupiter, accommodated to the former Periods of. For as Jupiter accedes to the Sun, the Shadow increases; and as he recedes from the Sun, it decreases. But this Equation is so inconsiderable, that it sizy most fafeiy be omitted. There is added also, as there ought, a Tablet, hewing the Half Duration of the Satellite in the Shadow of Jupiter according to the different Position of the Satellite with re - speech to the Nodes and Limits: For though, as was ( aid above, the Angle of the Inclination of the Plane of the Satellite ’ s Orbit be not great, Tis yet something -: And therefore about the Nodes of the Orbit the Xmmerfion will be more i direst and deep in the Shadow, than about the j Limits t And these Tables, together with the J U P common one of the Equation of Time, and no other, according to Mr. Halleys Judgment, are to be used in the Calculation of the Eclipses of this Satellite. In order to Calculation then, . From the Table of the Epoch of the Revolu - tions of the first Satellite to the Shadow of Jupi - ter ( which you will find amongst the Astronomy - cal Tables, under those Words in this Vol.. ) find first the Tear in the Left Hand Column, and then write down the Numbers that stand against it, expressing the Days, Hours, Minutes, and Se - conds of the Revolution: And also those in the other two Columns, N., N.. Under these Numbers place also in their proper Order ( from the next Table ) those which belong to the Month and Day assign ’ d, with those also in the little Co - lumps, N., N.. And then add them all fe - verally, as they stand in order, into one Sum. Then will the first of those Sums hew the mid - dle Moment of the Middle of the Eclipse: The Second serves for the first Equation: The Third finds the second Equation; that is, if you write down also in every Leap - Tear, and in the Months of January and February, the Day next after the given one, instead of the given Day, with its E - equations: For the Table accommodated, as it Ihouid be, to the greater Part of the Leap - Tear can ’ t serve without Correction for the former Part of the Tear, before the interposed Leap Tear Day. . If the Number placed in the former Co - lumn, and appointed for the former Equation, be less than ( the Half of the greatest ) that greatest Number itself also, if it be needful, being, as the entire Circle, first omitted, go to - the next following Table, agreeing to that Equa - tion ‘ and add the Equation there placed to the middle Time of the Eclipse before found: If the Sum exceed the Half of the greatest Num - ber, fubtraeft the Equation corresponding to it, from the middle Time of the Eclipse: Then will the Sum in the former Case, and the Difference in the latter, give you the Time of the Middle of the Eclipse, Equated the first Time. . If the Number placed in the latter Column, and either increased by the Eleventh Part of the former Equation, where the first Equation was found by Subtraction; orleffen ’ d by it, where it was gain ’ d by Addition; be less than, the Half of the greatest Number. ( draw greatest also it self, where ’ tis necejfiTary, being quite re - jected ); Then take that very Number, or if it be greater than the fame Half its Complement to the greatest Number, and apply it to find the fe - cond Equation; and add the proper correspond - ding Numbers, taken out of the Table, to the firli Equated Time of the Middle of the Eclipse. So hall the Sum of both be the true Moment of the Middle of the Eclipse. From which Moment ol Time if you subtract the Half Duration of the fame Eclipse ( taken easily out of the next following Table ) you will have the Moment of the Immersion; if you add it to that Time, you will have the Moment of the Emersion, and both duly accommodated to the mean Time of the Eclipse. This Jury is not only used in Circuits of Justices Errant, but also in other Courts and Matters of Of - sice: And though it appertains to most Courts of the Common Law; yet it is most notoriously in the Half - year Courts of the Justices Errants, com - monly called, the Great Affixes; and in the Quar - ter - Sessions, and in them it is most ordinarily cal - led a Jury, and that in a Civil Cause; whereas in other Courts ’ tis usually called an Inquest, and in the Court - Baron, a Jury of the Homage. In the General Affile there are usually many Juries, because there be ftoreof Causes both Civil and Cri - minal commonly to be tried; whereof one is cal - led, The Grand Jury, and the reft Petit Juries; where - of itfeemeth there should be one in every Hundred. The Grand Jury consists of Twenty four Grave and Substantial Gentlemen, or some of the better fort of Yeomen, chosen indifferently by the Sheriff out of the whole Shire, to confider of all Bills of Indidment preferred to the Court; which they do either approve, by writing upon them, Billa Vera; or disallow, by indorfing Ignoramus. Such as they do approve, if they touch Life and Death, are fur - ther referred to another Jury to be considered of, because the Case is of such Importance; but others of lighter Moment, are upon their Allowance, without more Work, fined by the Bench except the Party traverse the Indidment, or challenge it for Insufficiency, or remove the Cause to a higher Court by Certiorari; in which two former Cafes it is referred to another Jury; and in the latter, transmitted to a higher: And presently upon the Allowance of this Bill by the Grand Inquest, a Man is said to be indited: Such as they disallow are delivered to / he Bench, by whom they are forth - with canceled or torn. ' The Petit Jury consists of Twelve Men at the least, and are impannelled as well upon Criminal, as upon Civil Causes: Thole that pass upon Often - ces of Life and Death, do bring in their Verdid, either Guilty, or not Guilty; whereupon thePri - sooner, if he be found Guilty, is said to be Convic - ted, and so afterwards receiveth Judgment and Condemnation or otherwifeis acquitted and fet free. Those that pass upon Civil Causes Real, are all, or lo many as can conveniently be had, of the lame Hundred where the Land or Tenement in Question doth lie, being four at the least; and they, upon due Examination, bring in their Verdid either ior the Demandant or Tenant.

identity.c: IDENTITY: The Idea ’ s of Identity and Di - versify come into our Minds by the Power it hath of comparing the very Beings of Things where - by considering any thing, as existing in any de - terminer Time and Place, we compare it with it self existing at another time '; and accordingly pronounce it to be the fame ordiverfe. When we fee any thing to be in any place in any Infant of Time, we are sure ( be the thing what it will ) that it is that very thing, and not another: For what ever is another thing, must at that fame time exist in another place, how likefo ever it may be in all other refpeds. And in this consists Identity, when the Idea ’ s it is attributed to, vary not at all from what they were that moment, wherein we confi - der ’ d their former Existence, and to which we com - pare the present: for never finding nor conceiving it possible, that two things of the fame kind should exist in the fame place at the lame time, we right - ly conclude, that what ever exist any where at any time, excludes all of the fame kind, and is there it self alone. When therefore we demand. Whether any thing be the fame or noriltalways re - fers to some thing that exifted at such a time in such a place, which. Was certain, at that instant, was the fame with it self and no other. From whence it follows, that one thing can ’ t have tm Beginnings of Existence, nor two things one; it being impost - sable for two things, of the fame kind, to be or exist in the lame instant, in the very fame place; or one and the fame thing in divers places. What - ever therefore had one Beginning is the fame thing; and that which had a differentBeginning in Time and Place from that, is not the fame with that, but different from it. We seem to have Idea ’ s but of three forts of Substances, GOD, Finite Intelligences or Sprits, and Bodies. Of G O D, ’ tis demonstrable that He is without Beginning, Eternal, Unalterable, and Omnipresent; wherefore of His Identity there can be no doubt. Finite Spirits having had each its determinate Time and Place of Beginning to exist; the Re - lation to that Time and Place will always determine to each of them its Identity, as long as it exilts. And the fame will hold of Bodies. And in eve - ry Particle of Matter, to which no Addition or Subtraction of Matter being made, it is the fame. And though these three forts of Substances do not exclude one another out of the fame Place; yet we cannot conceive but that they must neceflari - - y each of them exclude any other of the fame kind, out of the fame Place; or else the Notions and Names of Identity and Diversity would be in vain; and there could be no such Diftincftion of Sub - stances, or any thing else from one another. Thus, v. gr. if two Bodies or Particles of Matter could be in the fame place at the fame time; then take them, great or little, they must be one and the fame; nay, thus all Bodies must be one and the fame. ’ Tis plain then that the so much disputed Prin - cipium Individuationis is Existence it self; which determines a Being of any fort to a particular Time and Place, incommunicably to two Beings of the fame kind. And here it will do well to distinguish between dead and unaCtive Lumps of Matter, and such Bo - dies as those endow ’ d with Vegetable or Animal Life. If you confider one of the former kinds of Bodies; if it consist only of one, or a determinate Number of many Atoms, any way combined to - gether; while that one continues without mixture with others; or while the many exist, united toge - ther in the fame Mass, i t will still be the somebody; but if one Atom be taken away, or any new one added, it is no longer the fame Mass, or the fame Body. But in the State of Living Creatures / their I - density depends not on amass of the fame Particles, but onfomething else; for in them the Variation of great Parcels of Matter alters not the Identity. An Oak growing from a Plant to a great Tree; and a Child growing to an Adult Person, are still the fame; tho ’ in both Cafes there be a manifest Change of Parts: For here ’ tis such a peculiar Disposition and Organization of Parrs in one come - rent Body, and partaking of one common Life, that conftimtes their Identity; and as long as that continues, it will be the fame Oak or Man. And so it is in a Watch; as long as the Mechanism of it continues the fame, and it goes and answers the End of its Organization, ’ tis the fame Watch, tho ’ many Particles of Matter continually rub off and wear away. ’ Tis clear therefore wherein consists the Identity of any Animal or Vegetable. But there is another fort of Identity, which hath not been improperly called Personal; which S think Mr. Lock, truly determines to consist in the Sameness of a Rational Being; Since by Person we understand an Intelligent Being, having Reason and Reflection: And since there is a Consciousness which always accompanies Thinking it Is that which makes every one to be that, which he calls himself, thereby distinguishing him from all other Beings that think, and give him his Personal Iden - tity. incombustiblecloth.c: INCOMBUSTIBLE Cloth, is a fort of very odd Linen, made from a Scone in the form of a Talk; and call ’ d Lapis Ammanthus and Asbefto s, Alumen Plum ofum. Folia, Corsbides, Sparta Folia, ' Tis found in many places in China, Italy, and Wales and I have had a very clean fort, which would part into pretty long Threads, which was found in Scotland. The Incombustible Cloth made from this Mineral, is called Linum Vivian, Linutn Fojjile, Linum Indicum, Creticum, Cypri - sum, & &. from the Places where ’ tis found. This was of such esteem among the Ancients, as to be rank ’ d ( as Dr. Plot tells us ) with the most precious Pearls: And in China a piece of it but Inches long was valued at Tale, i. e. l. f. d. Pliny tells us expressly, and of his own knowledge, That Napkins of this Cloth being taken foul from the Table at a great Feast, where he was a Guest, were cast into the Fire, and by that means came out fairer and gleaner than if they had been wafli ’ d in Water. March Antonio Caftagna, Superinten - dent of some Mines in Italy, faith ( in Phil. Trans. N. J that causing a kind of Paper to be made of some of the Amianthus which he found there; k would abide longer in the Fire without being consumed than Plates of the hardest and most so - lid Metal; which would have scaled oft ' in Flakes with a much less Hear. Mr. Edward Lloyd also, in Numb.. gives an Account of some that he found in Wales, which remain ’ d in the Fire above a Quarter of an Hour without any Signs of be - ing consumed. Butin two Trials which were made before the Royal Society of a Piece of this Cloth of a Foot long, and half a Foot broad, and weighing about an Ounce and half; it was found to lose in a strong Fire, where it continued for several Mi - nutes, above a Dram of its Weight at a time. Of this Cloth, as Pliny informs us, flirouds were anciently made, and used at Royal Obfiequies to wrap up the Corps in, that the Allies of their Bodies might be preserved distend from those of the Wood, which constituted the Funeral Pile. And we are assured, that the Princes of Tartar use it for the fame purpose to this Day. And some of the ancient Indian Brachmans are said to have made themselves Cloaths of it. They tell us alio, that the Wickj for the Ancient ’ s Perpetual Lamps ( if there were any such thing ) were made of the Threads of this Alumen Plumofium, or Asbefion. Marcus Pau ’ us Venetus acquaints us. That one Curficar a Turn, a Superintendent of the Mines in the Tartarian Province of Chinchinthalas, assured him that they first dried this Mineral ( found there in a certain Mountain ) in the Sun; then pounded it in a Brass Mortar, to separate the Earthy part from it; and that afterwards it was also washed from all remaining Filth; and then was spun into Threads like Wool, and afterwards woven into Cloth; which, laid he, when spotted or foul they clean fe by throwing it into the Fire for an Hour ’ s time, whence it comes out unhurt, and as white as Snow. IN COMPOSITE Numbers, are the fame with those Euclide calls Prime Numbers. inferiorplanets.c: INFERIOR Planets are Mercury and Venus, so called, because they are next the Sun, the Cen - tre of the Planetary System. An Account of their Motion and Phenomena to an Eye placed at the Earth, is as follows. . The Periodical Times of their Motion thro the Ecliptick are plainly equal; which is contra - ry to what appears in the Motion of the Superior Planets: and their Progress through the Ecliptick is measured by the Motion of the Sun; so that if the apparent Motions of the Sun, Venus, and Mercury be considered for many Years toge - ther, they will appear to run through the Zodiac in an equal Space of Time. The Reason of this Diversity between the Su - period and Inferior Planets, is not from any real Difference in their Motions, but arises solely from the difterentPofition of thisEarth which reinhabit. All the Planets are circulated round the Sun in one and the fame ' Ratio; the more difiant requi - ring a longer time for their Revolution, than those which are more near. Thus the Earth be - ing farther from the Sun than Venus, is a longer tirjpe in moving round him; and Venus than Mer - cury: And to an Eye placed in the Sun the Mo - tions of the Inferior and Superior Planets would appear alike uniform and proportionable to their Distance. But to an Eye at the Earth, as the Superiors, containing our Orbit within theirs, will appear to move some times flower, and some times swifter; now to be Stationary, and now Re - trograde; so the Motions of the Inferiors will ap - pear to depend upon the Motion of the Sun, to whom they are so nearly joyned as it were; and to us, that are in an Orbit so far without them, will appear to be equal to the Motion of that Great Luminary. a. The Sun, Venus and Mercury, singly confi - dered, are each affeered with such an, Inequality of Motion, that it is very rare for them all three, or indeed for any two of them, to agree in the, fame Degree of Velocity. Indeed, Venus and Mercury had no Motion of their own round the Sun, but kept an invariable Position with regard to him, it were reafonableto suppose, that they should move on, aim oft. equa - bly, as the Sun doth. But since that apparent Motion with which they annually run through the Zodiac, is derived from a double Fountain; vis from their own proper Motion round the Sun, which is not very unequable in it self; and from the Position of the Earth, which is continually va - rious and changeable, in an Orbit that i without theirs, ’ tis not strange that each of the Inferior Platiets should appear to move unequally, and to go some times flower, and some times faster, by turns. . Although the Periodic Times at Venus and Mercury in the. Ecliptick, through the Course of the Year are thus accurately equal to one ano - ther, yet the Periodic Times o Venus, if reckon ’ d Q q q from I N F ] N F from any one present Position to the Sun, to a like subsequent one; if compared with the Periodic Times of Mercury in a like Position, Will appear to be of a much longer Length. For this Inequality of the Periodic Times, ac - cording to the unequal Distance from the Sun, " is agreeable to the established Law of the Heavenly Bodies: For Venus is nearer to the Sun than the Earth, and Mercury than Venus. Wherefore the Periodic Times of Veniis, considered in themselves, and with regard to the fix ’ d Stars, are not a little shorter than those of the Earth; and those of Mer - cury shorter than the Periodic Times of Venus. And though these Motions should be considered by a Spectator at the Earth, he would find in them the fame Inequality: For the Motion of Mercu - ry will be sooner, and oftner more swift, than that ' of the Earth and therefore their Periodic Times must be unequal. . These Inferior Planets are never either in Opposition or in Quadrature to the Sun; but al - ways more near to him, than to occasion those Phenomena For Mercury goes no farther from the Sun than about z Degrees, and Venus not a - above Degrees; some times to the Eastward, and some times to the Weft ward. That neither of these Planets can come to be in Quadrature, muchlefs in Opposition to the Sun, will be plain from the following Scheme. Let the Circle B FC E be the Earsh ’ s Annual Orbit; ADGIJ. the Orbit of Venus j and NM that of Mercury. The greatest Elongation of Ve - nus from the Sun is determined by the Acute An - gle L B A, made by the Line B L drawn from the Sun to the Earth, and the Lin e lM, which is a Tangent, to the Orbit of Venus. In like manner the Acute Angle LBN will determine the great - test Elongation of Mercury from the Sun. Now the Quantity of these Angles, in a Proportion af - sign ’ d, may be had from the Semidiameters of the Orbits being found by Observation, and by Tri - goniometrical Calculation: Or, indeed, they will be discovered by Observation of the greatest Elon - nations themselves. . Our Modern Astronomers have observ ’ d, That Venus appears bigger when Ihe begins to. re - cede from the Sun towards the East, and when Ihe is yet but a little distance from him but, on the contrary, that file appears less in her Ap - roach towards theSun, and when file comes pretty near him: Whereas, when she recedes from the Sun towards the Weft, then file appears less; but when she approaches towards him again, file again appears larger: And the fame things have been observed of Mercury, by the ule of long and good Telescopes. These Phenomena have quite over - turn ’ d the Ptolemaick. System of the Heavens; and may be accounted for thus: Since ail the Planets, as well as the Earth, are Opake, Scabrous, and Spherical Bodies, reflecting every way from them the Rays of the Sun failing upon them: ’ Tis plain, that that Hemisphere of any Planet only, which is turned towards the Sun, will be enlightened the other Half of it remaining in Darknels. And, since also an Observer here can only lee that Half or Hemisphere of any Planet, which is obverted, or turned towards the Earth, where he stands; if it be considered what Part of Venus is enlight - ten ’ d by the Sun, in her different Position or Si - tuition towards him; and what Part is seen, by an Eye at the Earth, in its Annual Orbit B FC E ( See the preceding Fig. ) It. will be plain that Ve - nus must appear leaf to us when she is in R; Be - cause, tho ’ slie be then the most near to us poflibie, yet her obscure Hemisphere being towards us, there will be but very little of her enlightened part seen: But when file comes into the Position D, rn n I N F I N F then some part of her illuminated Disk will be turned towards the Eye in B but a much great - ter part of her Obscure or Dark Hemisphere. And since sic is of a Spherical Figure, which to a distant Eye appears as a Plane, us clear that the Illuminated part of her Disk must appear in the form of Horns, turned from the Sun, or towards the Weft. And this is her Appearance when Venus is our Morning - Star, as hie is commonly called. But this Planet moving on in her Orbit to G, very near one half of her illuminated Disk will become visible to the Eye at B; and, con - sequently file will then appear in the form of an Half Moon. When file comes into the Position O, more than half of her enlighten ’ d Hemisphere will be visible, and so file will appear Gibbofe: And when file arrives at that Part of her Orbit which P designs, to an Eye at B, as before, file will appear, as we fay of the Moon, at Full that is, all her illuminated Disk will be visible. The fame kinds of Bases Venus will put on, as die moves forward in her Orbit through R, FI, A That is, in RShe wil be Gibbofe in H like an Half Moon in A Horned again but her Horns will be turned a contrary way to what they were, in D that is, now to the Eastward, but still from the Sun: And this is her Appearance when She is the Evening - Star. The fame kinds of Phenomena belong to Mer - cury respect being had to his particular Orbit and Period of his Revolution. But here we must take care that we be not de - ceiled by the General Consideration of her Phases only, so as to think that Venus will always appear brightest and largest in P, or in Qor O. The Appearance which Venus may seem to have in her Oppofjticn, as it may be called in P, will be quite altered by her coming as near as She can to the Sun: And as to the Places O and R, tho ’ Venus will fliine with near a full Face yet fire will be then so far from the Earth, that her Di - fiance from us will more than compensate for the Quantity of her Light: Wherefore you may ex - - prist to lee her appear most bright and splendid when She is in D or A. For fuppofeher to move from To FI then will some part of her Lucid Hemisphere be turned from us in B, and so can - not be seen and yet the remaining luminous Part comes still nearer to the Earth: And since her Shining, or apparent Light, increases in a Duplicate Ratio, or as the Square of her Distance from us dimininifhes, her Light will be much more increased by her Approach to the Earth than it will be lessened, by our seeing less of her ilium i - ted Disk. So alio suppose her to move from H to A, or yet farther on here still the Quantity of her illuminated Part decreases, but the duplicate Increase of her Approach to the Earth, will yet make her Splendour increase. But between A and R, the Decrease of her visible Light will be greater than what her Access towards the Earth can compensate and so her Light will continue - ally diminish more and more, till She will fet Heliacally, and so become invisible. Thus also while the Planet is moving from P towards her Approach towards the Earth in B is inconfide - ble, in comparison of the Parts of her illuminated Disk, which will be turned away from us and consequently, She will appear more obscurely in j than She will in P; But between and H, and so towards A, her Approach to the Earth will Vol, II. very much increase her Splendour, tho ’ less and less of her Lucid Disk become still visible. And from the Whole it is plain, that while She is mo - ving in the Arch H A, she will appear brightest and largely . The greatest Elongations of Venus, whether towards the East or Weft are unequal, and must be express ’ d by an unequal Number of Degrees. And the fame thing is also true of Mercury. This Phenomenon hath a double Original or Cause for it depends on the Excentrieity of the Orbits, both of Venus and of the Earth. For if the Distance LA ( in the former Fig. ) of Venus from the Sun or if L B, the Distance of the Earth from the Sun, be unequal it cannot be, but that the Angle LB A, in the Triangle LBjA, which is called the greatest: Elongation, must al - so be unequal: And indeed both those Lines are fubjebl to such an Inequality. . The fame Directions, Stations and Retro - gr delations which we observe in the COurfeofthe Superior Planets,; are found to belong to these In - serious and with the fame Circumstances of of Change. For suppose the Earth, as before in B, and im - moveable there, and the Planet in P ’ tis then plain, that while the Planet moves Easterly from P to ), to an Eye placed in B, it must: appear Diretl, or to move in Confequentia, as theyfpeak: That is, according to the Order of the Signs: And lo it will appear to do till it come to A. inflexion.c: INFLEXION of the Kays of Light. Sir Isaac Nevoton, in his Excellent Opticas, Book. makes thele Experiments and Observations on this fur - priming Phenomenon. . That in a well darken'd Room, a Hole, whose Diameter was of an Inch, being made with a Pin in a Plate of Lead, to let in the Sun ’ s Rays; he found that the Shadows of Hairs, Threads, Pin:., Straws, &c. placed in that Beam of Light, were very considerably broader than they ought to be, if the pays of Light had passed ion by those Bodies in Eight Lines: And for In - Ranee, that the Hair of a Man ’ s Head, whose Breadth was about the th part of an Inch, did at the distance of Foot from the Hole, and Inches from the Hair, call a Shadow which was a th part of an Inch broad, or four times its own Breadth: At Foot from the Hair, the Shadow was ten times as broad as the Hair; and at the distance of o Foot, it was runes as broad. And he found, that it was not material, whether the Hair was encompassed with Air, or with any other pellucid Substance For if the Hair were placed between polished Glasses, with Water between them, the Shadows were all one; as were alio the Shadows of Scratches made on the Surface of polished Plates of Glass, and of the Veins of such Glasses: And therefore the great Breadth of these Shadows must arise from some other Cause than the KpfraSion of the Air. It is plain also from this " Experiment, that the Kays are bent, and turned aside, in palling by the Hair, Sc. and, that the Hair ads on the Rays of Light at a good distance as they pass by it. And he Ihews, that the Adion is strongest on the Rays which pass by at the least Distances, and grows weaker as the Rays are further from it. . He observed that the Shadows of all Bo - dies in this Light ( were border ’ d with parallel Fringes of colour ’ d light; whereof, that next the Shadow, was luminous: It was difficult to distinguish the Colours, unless the Light pass ’ d very obliquely on a White Paper, and then they exi - bited Colours in this orderfrom the Shadows, vi. Violet, Indico, Pale - Blue; Green, Yellow, Red Blue, Yellow, Red Pale - lue, Pale - yellow, Pale - red. . He took accurately the Measures of these Fringes, which he there gives in a Table. And in the th Observation he slews, That the Breadth of the Fringes ( when cast obliquely on a smooth White Body ) seem ’ d to be in the Prcgref. sion of the Numbers, J -, Vt; aRd their In - tervals in. the fame proportion with them: i. e. the Fringes and their Intervals together to be in the. continued Progression of. - so, yf f, Or thereabouts. . The Sun Alining into a darkened Room thro a Hole, of an Inch broad, at or Foot from it, he placed a Sheet of Paftboard, black ’ d well all over; and which had in the Middle a Hole a - bout of an Inch square, for the Light to pass through. Behind the Hole, on the Paftboard, he fastned with Pitch the Blade of a fiiarp Knife, to intercept some part of the Light which passed through the Hole. Both Paftboard and Knife were placed perpendicular to the Rays of Light. Then placing the Paftboard so that ail the Light fell upon the Hole in it, and part of it on the Blade of the Knife there placed, while the other Part went by the Edge. He let that Part which passed by, fall on a white Paper, cr Foot be - yond the Knife; and there saw Streams of faint Light Jhoot out both ways from the Beam of Light into the Shadows like the Tails of Comets. Their whole Length, measured upon the Paper at the distance of Foot from the Knife, was about or Inches; so that they subtended an Angle at the Edge of a Knife of about Degrees. . He placed another, by the former; so that their Edges were parallel and look ’ d towards one another; so that a Beam of Light might fall on both, and some of it pass through between them. And when the Distance between their Edges was about the th part of an Inch in breadth, the Stream of Light thar passed through parted in the Middle, and left a Shadow between the two Parts: And this Shadow was so black and dark, that all the Light which passed between the Knives, seem ’ d to be bent and turned aside to the one hand or the other. As the Knives ap - roach ’ d, the Shadow between the Streams of Light grew frill broader; till at last, on their Contact, the whole Light vaniftred. Hence I gather ( faith he ) that the Light which is left bent, and goes to the inner Ends of the Streams, passes by the Edges of the Knives at the greatest distance: And this Distance, when the Shadow begins to appear between the Streams, is about the Zooth part of an Inch And the Light which passes by the Edges at less Distances, is more bent, and goes to those ' Streams which are further from the di - rest Light. . The Fringes above - mention ’ d, also appear ’ d in this Experiment. And lie gathers from this and the former Observation, that the Tight of the first Fringe passed by the Edge of its Knife at a Distance greater than the th part of an Inch; and the Light of the two or three Fringes at still greater Distances; and cpnlequently, that the Rays which caused the Streams of Light, palled nearer to the Knives Edges, than any other. . Two Knives, whole Edges were ground truly strait, were placed so ( by sticking their Points into aBoard, with their Edges towards one ) another as to make anAngleof above i. '. Here through a Hole, the th part of an Inch wide, the Beam of Light was let into the dark Room; which made the Fringe appear, at the distance of or Foot from the Hole, and on a Ruler held obliquely, at the distance of half an Inch from the Knives, parallel to the Edges of the Sha - dows, and without growing sensibly broader till they met in Angles equal to that made by - the Edges r N F fc. But when the Ruler was plac ’ d at a much. g ? earn - distance, the Fringes grew broad - der as they approached, and after meeting crolsd one another, and then grew yet much broader. . From hence he concludes, That the Dijlances at which the Fringes pass by the Knives are not increased nor alteredhy the approach of theKnives; but that the Angles in which the Rays are there bent, are much creased by that approach. And also, that the Edge of the Knife, which is nea - reft any Ray, determines vebieb way the Ray Shall be bent, and the other Knife increases the Flexure. In observing, . He found, that when the Fringes of the Shadows of the Knives fell perpendicularly on a Paper at a great distance from the Knives, they were in the form of Hyperbola s. . When he placed a Prism at the Hole ( made with a small Pin ) to refraCt the Light, he found that the Shadows of all Bodies held in the co - lour ’ d Light, between the Prism and the Wall, were bordered with Fringes of the Colour of that Light only in - which they were held: And also, that the Fringes in the Red Light Were largest, and those in Violet, leaf. Wherefore, the Rays which made thele Fringes in the Red Light, pass ’ d by the Hair, at a greater distance, than those which made the like Fringes in the Violet: And consequently theHair in causing these Fringes, aXs alike on the Red Light, or least refrangible Rays at a greater distance; and on the Violet or most refrangible Rays, at a less distance, and by those Atlions disposed the Reff Light into larger, and the Violet into smaller, and the Lights of in - termediate Colours into Fringes of intermediate Bignefles, without changing the Colour of any fort of Light. When therefore theHair in the first and second Observation, being held in the com - mon white Light of the Sun, cast a Shadow bor - der ’ d with three Fringes of colour ’ d Light; those Colours ( ' tis plain ) did not arise from any new Modifications impress ’ d on the Rays of Light by the Hair, but only from the various Inflexions, whereby the leveral forts of Rays were separated from one another; which before Separation by the Mixture of their Colours, competed the White Beam of the Sun ’ s Light; but when ever sea - rated, compose Lights of the several Colours which they are originally disposed to exhibit. And this mightily confirms his Doctrine and The - ory of Colours, as indeed all kinds of Experiments and Considerations do: See Colours. These wonderful Properties of the Inflexion of the Rays of Light, are caused by a Body adding at a distance on the Rays: And yet this Action of In - flexion is the stronger, the less such distance is: So that perhaps the Attraction which causes it don ’ t exert its Sphere of Activity beyond such a distance. The Rays of Light also themselves, as they differ in Refrangibility, are diversly infleXed and separated into those three Fringes of Coloi rs mention ’ d by Sir If. Newton in his Excellent Op - ticks, Lib.. and before obferveci by Grimaldm, to arise from any small Bodies, such as Hairs, Wires, &c. placed in the Sun ’ s Rays, let into a well darkened Room, by a very small Hole, N N made only by the Point of a Needle in a Plate of Metal. And thele Fimbria, or colour ’ d Fringes, seem to be made by a kind of undulatory Motion or Inflection of the Rays; as they come near the Extremities of Bodies, the three different Co - lours of the Fringes, arising from three such dise - rent Inflections.

intestines.c: INTESTINES, are a long and large Pipe, which by several Turnings and Windings reaches from the Pylorus to the Anus: They are knit all along the Edge of a Membrane call ’ d the Mefen - tery, and are usually fix times as long as the Bo - ' dy to which they belong; that so the Chyle which escapes the Ladeals of one of the Guts may be taken up by - those in the next. They have three Coats, of which the inmost is made up of short Fibres bound together by fine Blood - Vessels, and disposed as those of the Stomach: For the Length of a Fibre is the Thickness of the Coat. This Coat being much larger than ths - thers, lies in Wrinkles or Plaits, which are call'd Valvulce Conniventes. It hath also a great num - ber of little Glands, which in the small Guts lie in clusters every where, but where they are knit to the Mesentery. These Glands seem to leap - rate a Liquor for the dilating of the thick Chyle, that it may the more easily enter the small Ori - fices. of the Ladeals. The second Coat is made up of two Orders of Muscular Fibres, one running strait, according to the length of the Guts the other goes round, describing rather a Spiral than a Circular Line. By the successive Motion of these two Orders of Fibres, the Guts are in a con - tinkal Undulation - which is call ’ d the Vermicular or PeriJlalticJ ' Motion of the Intestines. The third and external Coat is common, and comes from Peritoneum. The Intestines, tho ’ properly but one continued Pipe, yet are divided into Six Parts Three thin and small, and Three thick and great. The thin and small are the Duodenum, the Jejunum and Ileum. Thick and great Guts are the - Catcv. m, Colon, and PeSltim: See those W ords.

intestinemotion.c: INTESTINE Motion of the Parts of Fluids. Where the attrading Corpuscles of any Fluid are Elastick, they must necessarily produce an Intef - tine Motion and this greater or lesser, according to the Degrees of their Elasticity and attractive Forces For two Elastick Particles, after meeting, will fly from one another ( abftrading from the Rest - ance of the Medium ) with the lame Degree of Velocity that they met together with. ( See Ela - sticity. ) But when in leaping back from one a - nother they approach other Particles, their Velo - city will be encreased.

invest.c: INVEST: To Invest, in the Law, signifies to give Polfeifion: And the Action of doing this, which is attended in different Places with dise - rent Ceremonies, Forms and Customs, is called INVESTITURE.

jobenthails.c: JOBENT Hails, are a smaller fort, common - ly, used to nail thin Plates of Iron to Wood. J NT - Ti ? w / ? KtJ, are such as come to, and hold Lands or Tenements by one Title pro Indi - vis, or without Partition. These are distinguish ’ d from Sole, or Several Tenants, from Parceners, and from Tenants, in Common: And anciently they were called Parti - cipes, and not Heredes: And these must joyntly Implead, and joyntly be Impleaded which proper - ty is ’ common to them and to Coparceners. But Joint - Tenants have a some Property of Survivorship, which Coparceners have not: For if there be two or three Joint - Tenants, and one hath IlTue and dies, then he or those Joint - Tenants that survive, shall have the Whole by Survivorship.

joistsinarchitecture.c: JOISTS, in Architecture, are such Pieces of Timber as are framed into the Girders and Sum -, mers, and on which the Boards of the Floor are laid.

joinderinlaw.c: JOINDER, in Law, is the Coupling or Joyning pf two Persons in one Action or Suit a - gainst another.. JOYNTS: See JO ’ STS.

irregular.c: IRREGULAR ! i Y, in the Canon - Law, Sig - nifies an Impediment, which will hinder a Fer - sorts going into Holy Orders; as being a Bastard, Maimed, Confenting to a Murder, &c.

irrepleviable.c: IRREPLEVIABLE, in the Common Taw, signifies, what may not be replevied, or fet at Large, upon Sureties.

isochronal.c: ISOCHRONAL - LINE, is that in which a hea - vy Body isfuppoled to descend, without any Ac - celebration And the Excellent G. G. Leilmit, in the All. Erud. Lips. for Fehr... hath a Discourse on this Subject - in which he five ws, That an heavy Body, with a Degree of Velocity acquired by the Descent from any Height,, may descend from the fame Point, by an infinite Num - ber of Ifochronai - Curves, and which are., all of the fame Species, differing from one another only in the Magnitude of their Parameters; such as are all the Quadrato - Cubical Paraboloids, and conse - quently similar to one another. He shews also there how to find a Line, in which a heavy Body descending, shall recede uni - formly from a given Point, or approach uniform - ly to it. IS THMUS, in Anatomy, is a Passage in that part of the Medulla Oblongata of the Brain, which lies bee ween the Cerebrum and Cerebellum, ' and which reaches from the place called the Anus to the fourth Ventricle. The Upper - part or Cover of this Conduit or Passage, which is betwixt the Tefies and the foremost Vermicular Process of the Cerebellum, and to which two it is tied at its two Ends, and to the Processes that come from the Cerebellum to the Tefies at its Sides; is called Va lent Major: It is of a Medullary Substance; and its Use is to keep the Lympha from falling out a - above the Nerves in the B sis of the Skull,

italianhours.c: ITALIAN Hours, are the Hours of the Natural - Day, accounted on from the Sun - setting of one Day, to the fame time again the next Day, as ’ tis the Custom in Italy to do this day, and as the Jews did of old.

itinerantjudgesorjustices.c: ITINERANT Judges or Justices, are such as were formerly sent with Commission into divers Countries to hear chiefly such Causes as were called Pleas of the Crown, the fame with Justices in Eyre; which fee.

jubilee.c: JUBILEE, is a solemn Time of Festivity at Borne, in which the Pope pretends to give Pardons Indulgences, and Bleflings to such Rich Credulous Persons as have as much Mo - nt as Faith, and who have leisure enough to go thither to fetch them. ' The first Jubilee is said to have been Instituted by Pope Boniface VIII. A. D.. to return " every Hundred Years. But Pope Clement VI, Wrought such a Fair of Indulgences should be kept oftner; and so lie order ’ d that the Jubilee should return again eve - ry Fifty Years; which was Decreed A. D.. In Imitation of this profitable Pardon - Market at Bpme, the Monks of Christ ' s - Church in Canter - bury fet up a Jubilee of their own every Fiftieth year also, to get a Concourse of Fools to the Shrine of that Insolent Prelate Thomas Becked. Our King Edward. kept a kind of Civil Ju - bile at his Court in the Fiftieth year of his own Age; which was in; granting Pardons, Privileges, and other Civil Induigencies. JUDI - J U P

jusretrains.c: JUS Retrains five Retrovendendi, in the Civil Law, is an Agreement between Buyer and Sel - ler, that the latter and his Heirs may buy back the Goods or Wares again before any other.

juslice.c: JUS LICE. The Vertue of Justice is either Universal or Particular. General or Universal Justice is a constant giving to every one his Due - and this hath for its Object all Laws both Di - vine and Human. Particular Justice, is a con - scant Will and Desire of giving every one his Due, according to particular Agreement, or the Laws of Civil Society. Particular Justice, as ’ cis exercised in Commerce, is usually called Commu - tffwe, and fomenmes Expletory Justice, being directed without any regard to the different Con - ditions of Men, but observes the Simple Proper - tion, and is wholly bent on the Value or Price of Things, or what is really and justly due But if you confider Particular Justice, as it is ever - cifedin Governing, or in Beneficence, it is called Distributive or Attributive Justice and, is con - corn ’ d in the appointing of Rewards and Pfinifh - ments, according to the several Conditions, Sta - tions and Qualities of Men, according as they are more or less Good or Bad, Useful or Preju - dicial, Worthy or Unworthy. And when there are many Claimers for Rewards, it observes a Comparative Proportion. justicesoflabourers.c: JUSTICES of Labourers, were Justices here - tifore appointed toredrefs th e Forwardness of La - bourers, that would either be Idle, or have reasonable Wages.

justicesoftrailebaflon.c: JUSTICES of Traile Baflon, were a kind of Justices appointed by Edward the Fiift, on great Diforders arising in the Kingdom, while he was absent in the Scotch and French Wars. Their Office was to make Inquisition throughout the Realm, by the Verdidt of substantial juries, upon all Officers, as Mayors, Sheriffs, Bailiffs, &c. for their Breach or Negledt of Duty, in not Pu - nithing Bribery, Extortion, &c. ’ Tis molt like - ly they received their Name from a Bastion, or Staff that was the Body of their Office, as it is of a Mareschal of France: And who ever was brought before them was Traile d Ballon, tra - ditus ad Baculum, brought to the Staff of Justice. K A L ALENDiE, were formerly Rural Chap - ters, or Conventions of the Rural Dean and Parochial Clergy so called because they were held on the Kalends, or first Days, of every Month; as at first every three Weeks: At last these Conventions came to be held only once a Quarter and by degrees have been wholly in - permitted, to the great decay of Good Discipline.
